item.title: Expanding the public transport network. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s announcement to construct two monorail corridors across the capital by 2030 -- with BUET consultants completing pre-feasibility studies and detailed designs underway -- is certainly a welcome step in expanding Dhaka's public transportation network.
Designed to complement the existing Metro Rail and address last-mile connectivity in high-density bottlenecks, this appears a sensible undertaking to offer a viable, eco-friendly solution to chronic traffic gridlock that only seems to worsen in the capital.
Expanding mass transit has long been an absolute necessity for economic survival in the city, and it is good to see plans being developed to address it.
Yet, public enthusiasm for new transit infrastructure is inevitably tempered by a history of systemic mismanagement, and this apprehension is not without reason.
For decades, Bangladesh’s megaprojects have been plagued by a predictable blueprint of failure: Severe deadline extensions, rampant cost overruns, poor coordination, and opaque procurement processes that balloon into crushing public debts.
When major infrastructure ventures consistently double their original budgets, often as a result of incompetence, disregard, or simple administrative inertia, it is taxpayers who carry that unfair financial burden.
The proposed monorail initiative, and indeed subsequent infrastructure projects, must break decisively from this legacy of inefficiency. If this project suffers the same bureaucratic bloat and inflated expenditures that have tarnished past endeavours, its primary rationale will be completely compromised.
We must thus establish uncompromising governance from day one. The government must set firm, non-negotiable cost caps and strict timeline milestones, holding contractors and public officials accountable for any unjustified delays or financial leakages.
Building modern transit for Dhaka is a crucial step forward and has no alternative. However, it is doing it on time, within budget, and free of corruption that must be ensured.

Women entrepreneurs in particular can do so much more if given a level playing field. Tasking diplomatic missions with helping local women access global markets certainly points toward a visionary ambition, and we welcome it.
Yet, warm words and exhibition showcases will do nothing to alter economic realities unless the state backs them up with radical policy reform.
For decades, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and particularly women-led businesses, have faced an unforgiving wall of bureaucratic red tape, institutional indifference, and severe financial exclusion.
The harsh reality is that women entrepreneurs across our nation do not merely need diplomatic exposure but need the very basics to operate a business - collateral-free credit, simplified bank loan processing, and protection from predatory lending.
Commercial banks continue to treat women-led SMEs as high-risk ventures, demanding unreasonable collateral and drowning applicants in paperwork. While state agencies draft grand blueprints for export expansion, countless grassroots creators struggle simply to open a basic merchant account or secure working capital.
From operationalizing dedicated, low-interest loan windows specifically tailored for women entrepreneurs to eliminating the bureaucratic hurdles to providing genuine training, digital literacy, and logistical backing for these women, these are just a few ways we can begin to include more women in our journey to economic prosperity.
A trillion-dollar economy cannot be built on the backs of marginalized innovators who are starved of capital and suffocated by red tape. We must move swiftly from policy speeches to concrete financial delivery.
If the government genuinely intends to harness women’s economic potential, structural support must replace empty promises.

item.title: Feeding children is just good economics. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Economics divides itself into two. Macroeconomics is about how the whole economy works, and it's what we always see the talking heads on TV chattering away about. Inflation, the deficit, interest rates, and so on. Macroeconomics is also the part of economics we don't know much about, and much of what we think we do is wrong.
Microeconomics is the details of prices and markets and interactions between people. Much of what we know here is correct even if many people would prefer that it weren't. For many people would much prefer it if humans didn't go around acting so human all the time.
Those words, macro and micro, also give us a clue. Macro means large, micro small. So, if you want to be a big and important person -- or a talking head on TV -- then you'll want to lean on macroeconomics. You know, chatter on about the big stuff.
But the bit that really makes the difference to how life is lived is that small stuff. As is true in life itself of course -- it's the little things that make life enjoyable and worth living. Further, with micro, we can do experiments and really zero in on what actually works.
The news is that the Bangladeshi government has understood one part of this sort of research and is even doing the right thing about it. It's this : “The government's school feeding initiative is set for a major expansion in 2027, with plans to increase coverage from 3.1 million to around 11 million students at government primary schools across the country.”
We could just say that parents should feed their kids at home and that's that. We could also say that isn't it great that the kids get a lovely meal from the government? But that's not really the point or issue here, it's this: “Ensuring student attendance.”
A lot of research has been done on who sends their kids to school and why. One alarming result was that when child labour is made illegal, then fewer poor children go to school. The logic is that some people are so really poor that any child has to start work so that that child brings in enough money to feed that very same child.
Poor parents know that education is a good thing, it will make the children richer when they're older. But it is necessary for that child to survive long enough to get older.
Research shows that such poor families might well send one or some of the children to school and others have to go to work in order to bring in the necessary money to feed all of them. Of course, it will be more likely to be girls who are made to work while the boys learn to read and write.
If we make child labour illegal, then this will lower the wages the children can receive when working. This is obvious and logical as people will exploit those working illegally more than those working legally. If the wages of the children working fall, more of the children have to work to be able to feed all of the children.
Note that economics is not saying this should happen. It's certainly not approving of it happening. It's just noting that this does happen.
We'd prefer there to be no child labour, of course we would. But as we see, just making it illegal can actually increase the amount of it.
So perhaps we require a different way of achieving our goal?
One of the basic findings of that whole field of microeconomics is that people respond to incentives. In fact, Charlie Munger (he was Warren Buffett's partner) used to say: “Show me the incentive and I'll tell you the outcome.”
Another way of putting that same point is that we should try to tempt people to do the right thing rather than attempt to force them. You know, promising a toddler a sweetie often works better than slapping them in getting them to do something.
So, to restate the poor children and school problem. The parents can only feed the child if the child works, so therefore the child doesn't go to school and is thus trapped in lifelong poverty.
What if we feed the child at school? Then they will both be fed and also be educated? And this time, all the kids can go to school because all the kids will be fed.
This has been studied a lot. There are whole shelves of research in libraries on this. As far as anyone can tell, this works really well.
The World Food Program from the Americans pays for this in many countries and is going to help in Bangladesh. There's also a charity, Mary's Meals, which does the same thing for whole countries. The charity does it possibly better and certainly cheaper than the government, but that's another story.
We've got something that is going to make that future world better. Children will be fed, that's good, but also more children will gain more education.
I personally don't like macroeconomics but a lot of that is because I simply cannot get my head around the advanced mathematics used in it. A failing of mine rather than the subject perhaps.
But I also like this microeconomics because it provides answers to how to make the world a better place in simple, pragmatic, doable ways.
We can just feed every child at school. Feeding every child at school works, makes the world a better place in the future. So, we should do that then.

item.title: What makes growth inclusive?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In recent times, there are renewed talks on the notion of inclusive growth. One question that keeps on popping up is what makes growth inclusive.
Everyone agrees that sustained economic growth is central to the ability of countries to advance human development and tackle poverty over a long period of time. But sustained growth alone is not enough to advance human development. For that, growth needs to be inclusive.
Inclusive growth is characterized by three mutually reinforcing elements:
Sustained growth which is pro-poor ensures poverty reduction as well as reduction in inequalities. Equity in resources, services, and income not only leads to human capabilities and opportunities, but it is also crucial for fair and just societies.
When growth is accompanied by rapid increases in productive employment, the incomes of and opportunities for the poor are likely to increase. Productive employment enhances livelihood, participation, dignity, and voice.
All together, inclusive growth is a driving force for human development and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
To start with sustained growth is a prerequisite for inclusive growth. But sustained growth does not automatically become inclusive. In order to be inclusive, growth has to be pro-poor.
What is pro-poor growth?
The simplest notion of pro-poor growth assumes that so long as growth is associated with a reduction in poverty, it is pro-poor. The problem with this simple definition is that economic growth has largely been found to have some poverty-reducing impacts, at least through its trickledown effects. Thus, in terms of this simple definition, almost all economic growth is pro-poor.
The fundamental point, however, is that the “pro-poorness” of growth is not defined only by its poverty reduction impacts, but by the fact whether the poor actively engage in generating the growth, and also derive disproportionate benefits from it.
In other words, for growth to be pro-poor, the rate of income growth of the poor must exceed the rate of income growth of the non-poor and growth must accompanied by decreasing inequality.
While pro-poor growth is a necessary condition for inclusive growth, it is not a sufficient condition because it may not include non-poor people belonging to ethnic minorities, specific races, and so on. In many cases, these groups of people undertake economic activities which result in good livelihoods, but they have neither a voice in the decision-making process in the mainstream growth, nor are their activities integrated in it.
Equity remains at the heart of inclusive growth as distribution determines the pace, nature, and the pattern of growth. For growth to be inclusive, equity needs to be ensured on three planes:
If the production and the growth process start with an equitable distribution of assets, resources, and endowments, not only would they result in higher growth, but the benefits of growth are also equitably distributed.
When poor farmers have access to land and agricultural input packages, or small-scale entrepreneurs have access to credit, these not only enhance the growth process, but also ensure their fair share in it.
Infrastructure like roads, energy, transport, and communication has an economic activation effect, which implies new economic opportunities, better access to markets, and information. When poor people have access to such infrastructure, it makes growth pro-poor and inclusive.
Equitable access to basic social services, such as health and education and infrastructure, is another central factor for inclusive growth. The theoretical underpinning of this argument can be traced back to Amartya Sen’s work: Development as Freedom .
Inclusiveness effectively means eliminating the various “unfreedoms” experienced by individuals. According to Sen, people’s freedoms are enhanced through the provision of essential social services. Enhancing these freedoms is itself a precondition for achieving inclusive growth. An inclusive growth strategy, therefore, ensures that growth is promoted along with policies that enhance access to social services such as health and education.
In the realm of equity, redistribution of income is also associated with inclusive growth. This works on two fronts.
First , a redistribution of growth benefits the poor through enhancing their income, building their asset base, and enhancing their opportunities -- all of which ensure more inclusion of them in the growth process.
Second , a redistribution of income in various forms of social assistance to marginalized groups (eg, people with disabilities, older people), who cannot participate in the growth process, would provide social protection to them. These people are not part of the generation of growth but still become included in it as beneficiaries.
With regard to equity, two other observations may be pertinent in the context of inclusive growth.
First , equity is also a determining factor of the extent to which economic growth may impact poverty reduction. Initial inequality and changes in inequality are also important factors which can limit the extent to which poor people can participate in and benefit from growth.
Second , gender inequality impacts inclusive growth as well. Gender inequality in education and employment not only has a negative impact on economic growth, but it also adversely affects the pro-poorness of such growth. Also, significant gender gaps in access to agricultural productive assets and input such as land, fertilizer, and modern technologies seriously limit pro-poor growth.
Productive employment is a major driving force for inclusive growth. If growth is to be inclusive, it must be job-creating. This is because productive employment ensures people’s participation in the growth process, both as active agents as well as significant beneficiaries. And poor people can effectively be employed if economic growth is generated in sectors where they are concentrated and if labour-intensive technologies are used.
These linkages remind us of the importance of the sectoral composition of growth. The expansion of capital-intensive mining industries can result in jobless growth, making little impression on poverty. The incomes of the poor largely depend on the nature and extent of employment that economic growth generates.
It basically implies that not all growth is equally employment-intensive and there is no automatic link between economic growth and employment generation. Economic growth can be jobless, as the history of economic development has often shown.
Dr Selim Jahan is Former Director, Human Development Report Office and Poverty Division, United Nations Development Program, New York, USA.

The growing threat of unclean air. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dhaka's air pollution has once again reached alarming levels, with the capital recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 203 on Friday morning. Classified as “very unhealthy,” this reading is another reminder of a public health crisis that continues to receive far less attention than it deserves.
Air pollution is not a seasonal inconvenience that residents should simply learn to live with. It is a serious threat to public health, contributing to respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular diseases, and other long-term complications. Children, older people, and those with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable, but the consequences extend to everyone who breathes the city's air.
The sources of this pollution are well known: Unregulated construction, road dust, emissions from ageing vehicles, industrial pollution, and brick kilns all contribute to the problem. Yet, despite repeated warnings and directives, meaningful improvements remain difficult to see.
The courts have previously issued directives to tackle air pollution, including controlling construction dust and shutting down illegal brick kilns. The continued deterioration of air quality raises serious questions about how effectively these measures are being enforced.
We need more than occasional drives and temporary interventions. Authorities must coordinate their efforts, enforce environmental regulations and hold those responsible for pollution accountable.
Construction sites must follow dust-control requirements, illegal brick kilns must be shut down, and vehicle emissions must be monitored more strictly. Regular monitoring and transparent reporting should also become standard practice.
At the same time, improving public transport, expanding green spaces, and investing in sustainable urban planning must be treated as long-term priorities.
People should not have to choose between going outside and protecting their health.
Let us be clear: Clean air is a basic necessity, not a privilege. Dhaka's worsening pollution demands urgent, sustained action. Another day of alarming AQI readings should not remain another day of inaction.

item.title: We need more public-private partnership. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A healthcare system under unrealistic pressure like ours needs practical ways to improve the quality and reach of public hospitals, and this initiative, if implemented carefully, could address some of the gaps that have long undermined public healthcare.
Under the proposed pilot, private partners will provide services at five tertiary-level hospitals, with fees still to be finalized before the program begins.
The intention to expand the model to other cities is also encouraging. Public hospitals face shortages of equipment, specialized services, and trained personnel. Private expertise and investment could improve facilities, strengthen management, and give patients access to treatment that might otherwise be out of reach.
However, this partnership must strengthen public healthcare, not make essential treatment a privilege. Fees charged by private partners need to be reasonable and clearly disclosed. Patients should not face unexpected costs, and those unable to afford additional charges must not be pushed aside.
The government must set firm standards for service quality, monitor performance, and hold partners accountable for meeting agreed targets.
The initiative must also complement sustained public investment. Bangladesh cannot rely on private participation alone to resolve long standing weaknesses in healthcare.
Hospitals need adequate staffing, functioning equipment, regular maintenance and better management. Plans to recruit more doctors and expand critical care facilities must move forward without unnecessary delays.
The five-hospital pilot should be an opportunity to measure results and correct shortcomings before expansion. The government must publish clear information on costs, services and outcomes so the public can judge whether the program is working.
This is precisely the kind of practical initiative the health sector needs more of. With transparency, affordability, and proper oversight, partnerships can help deliver better care to more people.
The real test, however, will be whether patients experience meaningful improvements.

item.title: Men neither see nor listen to women. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Searching the Dhaka Tribune last week for a piece of my own, I came instead upon an essay I have not been able to put down: Shuchi binte Shahjalal’s The women are divine .
She opens with the old belief of the idol-makers: That a Durga is incomplete unless a little earth from a sex worker’s doorstep is worked into her clay -- for a man leaves his virtue at that threshold, and the ground there turns holy. The goddess cannot be finished without the woman’s soil; the woman herself cannot be let into the festival. The earth is holy, she writes. The person is not.
Let me say at once what I am and am not doing. I am a man, and this is a piece about men. I will not presume to explain to the women of my homeland a cage they have mapped, from the inside, far better than I can.
Shuchi has already said the essential thing, with a scholar’s range and a poet’s aim. I want only to add a footnote -- from the poet we Bengalis reach for whenever we wish to sound reverent about women, and whom, I have come to think, we never actually heard.
We are fond of Tagore as a worshipper of the feminine. We quote him at weddings and drape our daughters’ recitals in his songs. It is worth remembering, then, that at his most attentive, the Bishwakobi was not building the pedestal Shuchi describes. He was warning against it.
I have spent this autumn translating his love songs, one line at a time, and two of them will not now leave me.
The first is Bhalobeshe, sokhi, nibhrite jatone -- “Love me, and in the quiet shrine of your heart, write my name.” Midway, the lover makes a stranger, smaller request:
“Keep, with tender care, my chattering bird, in the courtyard of your palace.”
Read it slowly, and the bird is no ornament. The whole ache of the song is the plea that it be kept, tended, listened to.
In a second song, Tumi ki keboli chhobi -- “Are you only a picture?” -- he almost begs her not to harden into mere paint on a canvas, to be real and present, not an image he can hang on a wall and admire.
A century before our present arguments, Tagore had already named the two ways a man fails a woman: He stops listening to her voice, and he lets her freeze into an image.
Shuchi calls on Nazrul, who dared to address the barangana , the prostitute, as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her.
Let me call on the other giant, who stands, I think, exactly where she does -- on the side of the woman no one will look at or listen to.
Her essay is unsparing about what reverence costs, in life and in death. She recalls the roughly 1,500 women driven from the Kandapara brothel in Tangail in 2014, long after a High Court had ruled such evictions unconstitutional; the sex workers ridiculed when they report rape, because the society “cannot imagine a sex worker being raped”; and Hamida Begum, who in 2020 became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a proper Islamic burial -- after which the imam who prayed over her said he would not do it again, having been scolded by his neighbours.
Beside these, she sets the national figures she cites: By the counts of the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad and Ain o Salish Kendra, 786 women and girls raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before; and almost 22,000 cases of violence against women and children logged by police in a single year.
I will not borrow her numbers to decorate an argument of my own. I note only what she notices -- that behind each is a woman whom a society that sorts its women into goddesses and fallen women has filed under the second heading.
And I would underline, for every man who thinks himself devout, the sentence of hers that ought to be read aloud from pulpits: A society that calls its women mothers and then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist walks, has not forgotten reverence -- it has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
Here, let me add the one thing a lifetime in medicine has taught me, because it bears on her point that rape is treated as a stain on a woman’s honour rather than a crime against her body.
I have spent my working life with the human heart -- the actual muscle, four chambers, no holier in a saint than in a so-called fallen woman. A body keeps no ledger of honour. It bleeds the same, grieves the same, heals or fails to heal the same, whatever box the neighbours have assigned its owner.
When we treat a woman’s injury as a stain on her family’s ijjat rather than harm to her person, we are not being moral. We are staring at the honour and refusing to see the woman -- the same failure, once more.
So the answer, I think, is not less reverence but reverence that finally opens its eyes. Read generously, the idol-maker’s belief is almost holy: The goddess is made, in part, of the outcast woman’s earth; the divine and the discarded are the same clay.
The tragedy is only that we stop at the clay. We bow to the figure and walk past the person who gave it her soil.
Tagore points where Shuchi points. Keep the chattering bird -- do not cage it, do not silence it, bend down and listen. Do not let her become only a picture on the wall.
The cure for a goddess no one can bear to meet is not to break her into a “fallen” woman; it is to come down off our own certainty and stand beside her at the doorstep -- to see her face, and to hear her voice.
Shuchi binte Shahjalal has written the diagnosis. The least her countrymen -- and I mean the men -- can do is read it with our eyes open for once, and admit what it took a woman on the Op-Ed desk to say plainly.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, many still hiding their faces: Divine in theory, and in practice neither seen nor heard.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, where he practises medicine.

item.title: Five priorities for Bangladesh ahead of COP31. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has stood at the frontline of climate change. Rising sea levels, cyclones, floods, salinity intrusion, and heat stress have made the country one of the most climate-vulnerable nations in the world.
Yet Bangladesh has also become one of the world's most remarkable examples of climate adaptation and resilience-building.
Discussions on Bangladesh’s climate priorities ahead of COP31 took place during the 64th meeting of the Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) of the UNFCCC in Bonn from June 8-18. The Bangladesh delegation was led by the special assistant to the prime minister of the newly formed government. As in previous years, I had the opportunity to follow the climate discussions and negotiations at SB64 and engage in a dialogue with the special assistant on Bangladesh’s future climate strategies.
Our exchange highlighted an important opportunity: Moving beyond the narrative of vulnerability and positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in climate solutions.
Bangladesh’s experience, particularly in community-led adaptation and resilience-building, offers valuable lessons for the world. At the same time, the country has an opportunity to further strengthen its role in global climate action by combining adaptation leadership with innovation, collaboration, and strategic engagement.
Based on discussions and reflections from SB64, five priorities deserve particular attention as Bangladesh prepares for COP31.
Bangladesh's greatest climate success story is not found in international conference halls but in local communities.
Over the last decades, investments in cyclone preparedness, community-based disaster management, early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and local adaptation initiatives have dramatically reduced climate-related mortality and strengthened resilience across vulnerable regions.
These achievements are increasingly recognized internationally as examples of successful adaptation in practice.
However, Bangladesh has not always been effective in translating these experiences into global influence. Stronger documentation, monitoring, and communication of adaptation outcomes are needed.
Robust data demonstrating how local adaptation initiatives reduce vulnerability, improve livelihoods, and strengthen resilience can help position Bangladesh as a global knowledge leader.
At a time when many countries are struggling to operationalize adaptation goals, Bangladesh possesses evidence and experience that the world urgently needs.
Adaptation will rightly remain Bangladesh's highest climate priority. Yet adaptation and mitigation should not be viewed as competing agendas.
The most successful climate investments increasingly deliver both emissions reductions and resilience benefits. Renewable energy systems can strengthen energy security during climate-related disruptions. Nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration can simultaneously store carbon, reduce disaster risks, and protect livelihoods. Climate-smart agriculture can improve food security while reducing emissions.
By prioritizing mitigation projects that generate adaptation co-benefits, Bangladesh can strengthen its international position, attract additional financing, and demonstrate how developing countries can pursue integrated climate action.
Rather than choosing between adaptation and mitigation, Bangladesh can show how the two agendas reinforce one another.
Climate action is most effective when it is co-created. Bangladesh has a vibrant ecosystem of NGOs, community organizations, researchers, youth groups, social enterprises, and local governments working on climate issues. Yet these actors are not always fully integrated into national climate planning and implementation processes.
Future climate strategies should place greater emphasis on collaborative governance, participatory planning, and co-development. Citizens and local communities possess valuable knowledge about risks, vulnerabilities, and practical solutions. Their involvement improves both legitimacy and effectiveness.
International experience increasingly shows that climate transitions succeed when governments act not only as regulators but also as facilitators of collaboration between public, private, academic, and civil society actors.
As climate negotiations become increasingly complex, effective participation requires a diverse range of expertise.
Bangladesh has long been respected within the UNFCCC process, particularly on adaptation and climate justice. However, future negotiations will increasingly involve highly technical discussions around climate finance, carbon markets, technology transfer, loss and damage mechanisms, and implementation frameworks.
To maximize influence at COP31 and beyond, Bangladesh should continue expanding the diversity of expertise within its delegations. Alongside government officials, delegations can benefit from economists, scientists, legal experts, finance specialists, communication professionals, and experienced negotiators.
Strong climate diplomacy requires both technical knowledge and strategic negotiation skills.
Prepare for emerging carbon market opportunities
The operationalization of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating new opportunities for international carbon trading and climate finance.
Many developing countries are now positioning themselves to benefit from emerging carbon markets through high-quality mitigation projects, nature-based solutions, and capacity-building initiatives. Bangladesh should actively prepare for this evolving landscape.
This requires investments in institutional capacity, transparent governance systems, project development expertise, monitoring frameworks, and stakeholder engagement. Universities, research institutions, private sector actors, and local communities all have important roles to play.
If approached strategically, carbon markets could become an additional source of climate finance while supporting sustainable development objectives.
A new chapter
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that climate vulnerability does not prevent climate leadership. The country's achievements in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and resilience-building are recognized around the world.
The challenge now is to build on that foundation.
By showcasing community-led adaptation successes, integrating mitigation and resilience objectives, strengthening collaborative governance, enhancing negotiation capacity, and preparing for emerging climate finance opportunities, Bangladesh can help shape the global climate agenda rather than simply respond to it.
As the world prepares for COP31, Bangladesh has an opportunity to present itself not only as a country at risk from climate change, but as a country helping to define the solutions.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

item.title: Lost in translation? Japanese minister blames X for diplomatic embarrassment. [ dawn ]
item.description:
TOKYO: A Japanese minister blamed Elon Musk’s X social media platform on Friday for almost plunging him into diplomatic hot water, after its automatic translation feature implied he did not know the names of world leaders he was meeting.

Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa assured reporters that he knew the identity of the current prime minister of Bangladesh after a post with photos of the two included the name of ousted premier Sheikh Hasina in its translated version.

“This is actually a serious matter. It is possible that the Bangladeshi public might be left with the impression that, Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry does not even know who our (Bangladeshi) prime minister is,” Akazawa told journalists.

His original Japanese-language post on X on Oct 28, accompanied by photos, stated that he met visiting Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

But the platform’s machine-translation tool incorrectly changed the English version to make Akazawa seem to declare that he met Sheikh Hasina, who has lived in exile in India since an uprising in 2024.

Making matters worse, it was not the first time Akazawa had fallen foul of a translation snafu on the platform.

He said a similar mistake occurred after he posted about his online meeting with Kuwait’s Oil Minister Tareq Al-Roumi on Thursday -- with the automatic translation feature saying he held talks with Qatar’s energy minister.

Akazawa added that his translated post on a meeting with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also stated an incorrect name.

“I experienced this three times,” he said, appealing to X to fix the translation tool.

Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

We are running out of time. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest stark warning regarding our country’s rapidly fading demographic dividend should not be taken lightly, and must be treated with the seriousness it warrants.
For two decades, state planners have casually boasted about our youthful population as if economic prosperity were an automatic guarantee. Yet, as new data confirms, the window of demographic opportunity is closing at an alarming pace.
With our country set to transition into an "ageing" society next year and an "aged" nation by 2051, Bangladesh is running out of time. Failing to transform our young population into a highly skilled, productively employed workforce before the dependency ratio flips is an existential policy failure.
While there are numerous reasons for why we have essentially failed to capitalize on the gift that is our demographic dividend, it can primarily be attributed to systemic misdirection.
Over 84% of our workforce remains trapped in informal employment, where low wages, non-existent social protections, and minimal productivity reign.
Another notable failure is our inability to empower women, with female labour force participation languishing at a dismal 38% and effectively locking out half the nation's potential productivity.
Instead of building a knowledge-based economy capable of generating high-value formal jobs, successive policy failures have left our youth under-skilled, underemployed, and ill-prepared for what the future holds.
It is time to abandon rhetoric and immediately execute a comprehensive demographic strategy to make the most of the time we do have left.
The clock is ticking, and the window is closer to being shut than most realize. Failure to act now means our demographic dividend permanently collapsing into a demographic disaster.

item.title: Nourishing our future. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We certainly appreciate the government’s plan to dramatically expand the national school feeding program -- scaling coverage from 3.1 million to 11 million government primary school students across the country.
This is a deeply commendable initiative. Addressing primary education through the twin lenses of nutritional security and classroom retention is a progressive, essential strategy, and we can only hope for more decisions such as this.
In a country where child stunting, poverty, and post-primary dropouts remain severe challenges and have compromised our future, providing age-appropriate, quality meals in partnership with global experts like the World Food Program can transform the educational trajectory of millions of young citizens.
Indeed, the government correctly recognizes that learning outcomes cannot be separated from basic physical well-being. A hungry child cannot focus on foundational education.
Furthermore, incorporating community participation, specifically training local mothers in hygienic food preparation and distribution, adds a thoughtful layer of social empowerment and local oversight.
What is needed now is transparent implementation and execution of these plans. It is only then will this initiative boost attendance, combat malnutrition, safeguard child health, and foster genuine community ownership in our public education system.
Bangladesh’s policy landscape is littered with well-intentioned welfare schemes that stumbled as a result of corruption and disregard. Expanding coverage nearly fourfold will not be as simple as announcing the intention to do so.
Providing 11 million children with daily nourishment could be transformational for our country, but we must move swiftly from promises to implementation, ensuring that no child in Bangladesh is forced to choose between an empty stomach and an education.
The government has outlined a vision that deserves wholehearted public support. Now, it must deliver.

item.title: Shadow cabinet in Bangladesh: Why the opposition must move beyond a paper lineup. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Introducing a shadow cabinet to a nation that hasn't seen the practice since its post-1990 democratic transition is a welcome departure. Yet, rendering this institution functional and meaningful remains a distinct challenge. It is not an end in itself, nor can it survive as a goal-free pursuit.
Following the 13th parliamentary general election -- where the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) won a landslide victory and the Jamaat-led alliance became the main opposition -- Jamaat explicitly announced its willingness to establish a shadow cabinet on February 17, the very day its lawmakers took their oaths.
True to its commitment, the Jamaat-led alliance formally declared a shadow cabinet in late August this year, with the party head designated as the shadow premier.
Yet, what we have witnessed over the subsequent two months is not encouraging for a functioning shadow cabinet.
I would be glad to be proven wrong, but very few people in this nation of 170 million know who sits in this shadow cabinet or who holds which portfolio.
There has been little effort to introduce these shadow ministers to ordinary citizens. Neither has there been much activity to give the public confidence that the shadow cabinet is establishing checks and balances in our parliamentary system.
When a government enters its ninth month in office, it naturally falters on certain promises and deliverables, earning public criticism. This is normal in a democracy.
However, the shadow cabinet remains invisible and unfelt when it comes to political and intellectual engagement -- failing to confront governmental shortcomings or offer superior policy alternatives and governance directions.
For Bangladesh’s formidable opposition, merely announcing a shadow cabinet lineup is not enough. If they mean business, they must introduce their shadow ministers to the public and make these "ministers-in-waiting" familiar faces through their work.
This work must include providing critical analyses of government operations, scrutinizing policies pursued by different ministries and agencies, and publishing policy papers with better alternatives.
Otherwise, a "paper shadow cabinet" will end up being no better than having no shadow cabinet at all.
A shadow cabinet does not just oppose; it proposes. By presenting viable alternative budgets and administrative strategies, it elevates public discourse and gives citizens a clear picture of how an alternative government would rule.
Rather than offering generalized, vague criticisms, assigned shadow ministers must deeply analyze specific portfolios such as home affairs, foreign affairs, health, education, and finance.
Such an exercise would elevate the efficiency of lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, turning parliament into a venue for lively debate.
Burdened by a history of house-boycott culture, Bangladeshi voters have long yearned for a vibrant parliament where policies are vigorously debated to serve the people best.
In a functional system, a shadow cabinet is a team of senior spokespeople chosen by the leader of the opposition to mirror the official cabinet. Each member is appointed to lead a specific policy area for their party, questioning and challenging their counterpart in the government.
In this way, the official opposition presents itself as a credible government-in-waiting. Shadow ministers must directly question, challenge, and monitor the performance, policies, and spending of their government counterparts.
If Bangladesh’s current parliamentary opposition wants to translate its shadow cabinet initiative into meaningful action, it must formulate alternative manifestos and detailed policy proposals to show the electorate how it would govern differently.
Shadow ministers need to lead opposition responses during major legislative debates, push back against government bills in the division lobbies, and use parliamentary questions to pressure sitting ministers.
They must make the best use of parliamentary sessions, choosing strategic topics for debate and bringing forward motions to challenge the government.
Ideally, shadow cabinet members should act as the primary public spokespeople on television, radio, and in the press to critique government actions. This does not happen automatically. It requires a deliberate political process of grooming these designated members so they can outmaneuver government functionaries in public and press debates.
Politics in Bangladesh is historically adversarial and deeply polarized. The relationship between the ruling party and the opposition is often treated as a winner-take-all battle, leaving little room for the mutual recognition and institutional cooperation that a shadow cabinet demands.
Yet, in a parliamentary democracy, seats on both the treasury and opposition benches are inherently temporary. The party in power today may well find itself on the opposition benches tomorrow.
What must remain permanent is a commitment to robust institutional practices -- and a shadow cabinet system should be at the very heart of that foundation.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: A historic first: Abdul El-Sayed’s senate victory against all the big guns. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The American people have once again demonstrated that, in a democracy, the ultimate source of political power rests with voters -- not billionaires, wealthy interest groups or even the president of the United States.
The projected victory of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s US Senate election on November 3, 2026 is a remarkable demonstration of this principle. Despite sustained personal attacks, religious and racial prejudice, enormous financial pressure, and political maneuvering, El-Sayed defeated Republican candidate Mike Rogers in a closely watched contest. This makes him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
This outcome represents much more than an individual electoral success. It is a significant challenge to the influence of money, political establishment, and divisive rhetoric in American democracy.
El-Sayed entered the contest promising to transform politics by returning power to ordinary people and challenging a system in which wealthy donors and powerful interest groups exercise disproportionate influence.
A physician and former public health leader, with a brilliant track record of delivering health services, El-Sayed brought a distinctive perspective to the campaign. His understanding of the everyday problems facing American families, combined with his ability to communicate practical solutions, distinguished him from his opponents.
Rather than allowing the campaign to become dominated by personal attacks, he consistently returned to a few central messages: Putting money back into people's pockets, getting money out of politics, and ensuring healthcare for all.
He repeatedly said that America is big enough for all of us -- it does not matter how you pray or not pray at all. He said, many are not the reason for the increase in gas price. It is the wrong policies of the president that has made the lives worse for the average American.
His campaign slogan captured the concerns of ordinary voters. People should not have to struggle simply to buy groceries, purchase essential medicines, fill their cars with petrol, or send their children to school. These are basic necessities, he argued, and a prosperous country such as the United States should be able to make them affordable.
El-Sayed also made his opposition to unconditional American military assistance to Israel a central part of his political position. He argued that public money should be invested in the needs of American communities rather than supporting military actions that have caused immense suffering to Palestinians.
He did not support any funding to Israel that has committed genocide and war crime in Gaza. His position was politically controversial, but he maintained that voters had the right to demand accountability over how their tax money was spent.
Personal attacks and religious prejudice
Perhaps the most extraordinary feature of the campaign was the intensity of the attacks directed at El-Sayed by President Donald Trump. Instead of concentrating exclusively on policy differences, Trump repeatedly targeted the candidate's Muslim faith, name, and background.
Among the expressions Trump used were “radical jihadist,” “jihadist” and, “Muslim Brotherhood member.” He also accused El-Sayed of being “on the side of the terrorists” and told him to “go back to where he came from,” although he was born in Michigan. On another occasion, Trump deliberately called him “Mohammed” and declared: “I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want.”
Trump further suggested that El-Sayed would represent a security threat in the Senate, saying that he would be the only senator required to pass through a metal detector. El-Sayed responded with a sharp retort: He would be willing to go through a metal detector if Trump would agree to go through a lie detector.
Trump also attempted to associate El-Sayed with the imposition of Sharia law, invoked the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, and suggested that Jewish and Black voters would be foolish to support him.
Such statements raise serious questions about Islamophobia, racial stereotyping, and religious prejudice in American electoral politics. Political disagreement is a legitimate part of democracy, and candidates must be open to criticism of their policies and public statements. However, portraying a fellow American as a terrorist or a foreigner without credible evidence is fundamentally different from challenging his political program.
A candidate's religion or ethnic background should never be treated as evidence of disloyalty or a threat to national security. The American electorate's response to these attacks will be closely examined, particularly because the campaign attempted to make religious identity a defining issue in a contest that should have centred on public policy and the future of Michigan.
A campaign against corporate financial influence
Another major challenge facing El-Sayed was the extraordinary financial power deployed against him during the Democratic primary. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), through its affiliated political action committee, the United Democracy Project, spent close to $30 million supporting his primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, and opposing El-Sayed. This was reported as the largest investment the organization had made in a single electoral race.
El-Sayed nevertheless won the Democratic nomination. He repeatedly criticized the influence of outside money in elections and argued that political representatives should be accountable to their constituents rather than wealthy and corporate donors and powerful lobbying organizations.
The scale of the financial imbalance was striking. During the primary campaign, El-Sayed described himself as being outspent by approximately 11 to one. His ability to overcome that disadvantage demonstrated the strength of grassroots mobilisation and the appeal of a campaign focused on the cost of living, healthcare, and political accountability.
His victory should not, however, be interpreted as a rejection or approval of any particular religious or ethnic community. Criticism of a foreign government's policies and opposition to military assistance are legitimate political positions. The central democratic question is whether elected representatives should be influenced by ordinary voters or by powerful financial interests.
A broader message from Muslim and minority voters
El-Sayed's victory is part of a wider political development involving Muslim and minority representation in the United States. Muslim Americans have increasingly participated in electoral politics, sought public office and demanded that their concerns be addressed as part of the national political debate.
The election also demonstrated that candidates should not be judged by religious identity or ethnic background. Voters are entitled to evaluate their representatives on competence, integrity, policy positions and their ability to improve people's lives.
Both Congress Women Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) and Rashida Tlaib (Michigan) faced vicious racial and religious vilifications but have been re-elected with increased votes.
The attempt to use anti-Muslim rhetoric as an electoral weapon may therefore have produced the opposite of its intended effect.
Rather than allowing religious prejudice to dominate the debate, El-Sayed kept returning to issues that affect people across religious, racial and ethnic boundaries: Household expenses, healthcare, education, employment and the influence of money in politics.
Very wisely, he did not respond to any unhelpful distracting personal attacks despite repeated incitement by the President and his opponent.
A changing political landscape in Washington
The implications of the 2026 midterm elections extend beyond Michigan. Election projections indicate that Democrats have gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. If counting and certification are completed, this will significantly change the political balance in Washington and create a stronger congressional check on President Trump's administration.
A divided government -- or one in which the president's party lacks control of Congress -- can have substantial consequences for legislation, public expenditure, foreign policy and executive accountability. Congressional oversight will become particularly important in areas where presidential decisions face strong political or constitutional objections.
There is also a significant development concerning American assistance to Israel. On November 3, Trump said that the United States would end its approximately $4 billion in annual aid to Israel after 2026, while continuing arms sales and other forms of assistance if required. He described Israel as sufficiently prosperous to manage without the annual funding.
However, the existing US-Israel assistance agreement runs through 2028, and the practical and legal implications of ending the assistance earlier remain to be clarified. The announcement is particularly noteworthy given the growing public debate in the United States about the war in Gaza and the use of American taxpayer money.
People's power is the ultimate decider
Abdul El-Sayed's victory offers an important lesson for democracies everywhere. Money can purchase advertising, political influence and access to powerful institutions, but it cannot automatically purchase public trust. Presidential endorsement, political intimidation and personal attacks cannot guarantee electoral success.
The people of Michigan have sent a message that their economic security, access to healthcare and political future matter more than attempts to divide them through religion, race or ethnicity. El-Sayed's success also demonstrates that a candidate can challenge powerful interests by presenting a clear program, maintaining consistency and building a broad grassroots movement.
His victory does not mean that the problems of American democracy have been solved. The influence of wealthy donors, political lobbying, racial discrimination and religious prejudice will remain subjects of public debate. Nor does one election guarantee that campaign promises will be fulfilled. El-Sayed will now face the difficult task of translating his commitments into legislation and practical improvements in people's lives.
Nevertheless, his achievement is historic. It demonstrates that the power of ordinary people, when mobilised around shared concerns and democratic principles, can overcome formidable political and financial obstacles.
Ultimately, democracy belongs to the people. No president, billionaire, lobby group or political establishment can permanently stand above the collective voice of an informed electorate.
Professor Dr Shahjahan Khan OAM is an Emeritus Professor at the University of Southern Queensland, Australia; an Expatriate Fellow of the Bangladesh Academy of Sciences; and former Vice-Chancellor of the Asian University of Bangladesh, Dhaka.

item.title: ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
ICJ is due to rule on the Rohingya genocide case. Here's what you need to know

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 11/05/2026 - 11:06
UN's top court sets 19 November as date for landmark judgment in case brought by Gambia against Myanmar
Off

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a judgment that could see the court hold a state responsible for genocide for the first time.

Officials announced on Tuesday that the court's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, would read the judgment at a public sitting at the Peace Palace in The Hague at 10am local time on 19 November. 

The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal.

Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.

Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

The case, brought by the Gambia in 2019, concerns the Myanmar military's 2017 violence in Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh and involved widely documented massacres and rapes. 

About 1.2 million Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, now live in camps around Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement.

Myanmar has denied committing genocide, saying its forces were responding to insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa), whose attacks on police posts in August 2017 killed 12 security personnel.

Antonia Mulvey, an international human rights lawyer who investigated sexual violence against the Rohingya for the UN in 2017, told Middle East Eye's Expert Witness Podcast that horrific sexual violence was central to the Gambia's argument that genocide took place.

"One individual said to me, 'I was lucky, I was only raped by three men,'" said Mulvey, whose organisation, Legal Action Worldwide, now represents Rohingya witnesses in the case.

"They would rape women and girls in public, in front of their family members, in front of their children, in communal areas. I heard of mass gang rapes, sometimes up to 40 women and girls at the time."

What is the case about?

The Gambia accuses Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention during its campaign against the Rohingya from 25 August 2017. 

The operations were carried out under Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief. 

Myanmar at the time had a civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, but the military-drafted constitution left the armed forces outside its control.

In February 2021, Min Aung Hlaing overthrew Suu Kyi's government in a coup, and in April this year he stepped down as army chief.

He was later elected president by a parliament dominated by military-backed lawmakers, following elections organised by the junta.

Rohingya fled mass killings, rape and the burning of villages during what the military described as "clearance operations".

The case is a dispute between states, so the court will decide whether Myanmar as a state is responsible, not whether any individual is guilty. 

A finding against Myanmar would arguably add to international pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, whose move to the presidency is widely perceived as a bid for international legitimacy.

How did it start?

In 2018, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar concluded that there was sufficient information to infer genocidal intent and recommended that senior military officials be investigated and prosecuted for genocide.

On 11 November 2019, the Gambia filed its case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). 

The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
Read More »

It was the first time a state not directly affected had brought a genocide case before the court. 

The west African country relied on the principle that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld.

In December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi, then Myanmar's civilian leader, appeared at the court to deny the allegations. 

In January 2020, after finding “a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice to the rights” of the Rohingya under the Genocide Convention, the court ordered Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence.

The court rejected Myanmar's objections to its jurisdiction in July 2022, and heard the merits of the case from 12-29 January 2026, including closed-door testimony from Rohingya witnesses.

Eleven states have intervened: Belgium, Canada, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, the Republic of Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom.

Mike Becker, an assistant professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ, told MEE the judgment would be the first merits judgment in a case with large-scale intervention by third states.

"Cases like the Gambia v Myanmar have arguably sought to transform the role and function of the ICJ in contemporary affairs. The outcome here may determine whether that trend will continue," Becker said.

What are the arguments?

The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the Myanmar military's conduct. 

It relied on four acts listed in the convention: killing; causing serious bodily or mental harm; inflicting conditions of life calculated to destroy the group; and measures intended to prevent births.

Mulvey said the Gambia pointed to around 10,000 killings, which she described as a conservative estimate, and to decades of restrictions on Rohingya marriage, births, movement and access to healthcare.

Myanmar denies genocide. It argues the operations were a counterterrorism response to Arsa, that there is no direct evidence of intent, and that the UN fact-finding mission's reports should not be given evidentiary weight.

Myanmar has submitted 12 reports on its compliance with the 2020 order. The Gambia has said these give "no reason to conclude" that Myanmar complied.

Why is sexual violence central?

Mulvey said she documented a consistent pattern across the townships of Maungdaw, Buthidaung and Rathedaung, in which soldiers surrounded villages, opened fire, set homes alight and then selected women and girls for rape.

She said survivors described gang rapes carried out in public and in front of their families, women held in military camps for weeks, mutilation, and soldiers telling them: "We will kill you by raping you."

One woman told Mulvey she had been eight months pregnant when she was hanged from a tree and raped by nine men, most of them soldiers. Her unborn child died. Her account was included in the fact-finding mission's report and later read out at the ICJ.

The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda ruled in 1998 that rape can constitute genocide. The ICJ has accepted the principle, but has never found a state responsible on that basis.

Mulvey said such a finding would be "a landmark decision".

"It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice, such as before Bosnia and Croatia," she said.

Why does it matter under international law?

The judgment will be only the third time the ICJ has ruled on the merits of a genocide case, and the first in more than a decade.

In 2007, the court found that genocide was committed at Srebrenica but held Serbia responsible only for failing to prevent and punish it.

'It was the scale and the brutality of the sexual violence that we didn't see in previous cases before the International Court of Justice'

– Antonia Mulvey, human rights lawyer

In 2015, it found that genocide had not been proven in Croatia's case against Serbia.

Furthermore, how the court applies the “only reasonable inference” test is expected to be a central legal question addressed by the judgment. 

The test governs how genocidal intent, meaning the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part, can be proven when there is no direct evidence of it, such as an explicit order or policy document. In this case, it would require proving whether any explanation other than genocide could reasonably account for what happened in Rakhine.

The Gambia argues that the scale, pattern and brutality of the 2017 operations meet that test. 

It points to the mass killings, the systematic rape of women and girls, and decades of discriminatory policies against the Rohingya.

“Here we don’t have a physical document that shows that, but it was the whole pattern that we saw,” Mulvey said.

Myanmar argues that other reasonable inferences can be drawn, chiefly that its forces were conducting counterterrorism operations against Arsa.

At the January hearings, its counsel also argued that the military’s aim was to drive the Rohingya out of the country, not to destroy them.

Chris Sidoti, a former member of the UN fact-finding mission on Myanmar, told MEE that the ruling would also show how the court approaches establishing facts and the weight given to reports from UN human rights mechanisms.

"The International Court of Justice is not a fact-finding tribunal. It doesn't have an investigative arm, and mostly it makes decisions that are purely legal questions," said Sidoti, who now sits on the UN Commission of Inquiry on Palestine and Israel. "Here it's got a fact-finding task ahead of it."

Will the ICJ lower the genocide threshold?

In October, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz accused Navi Pillay, the Nobel Peace laureate and the ad hoc judge appointed by the Gambia, of "tipping the scales", saying she intended to lower the threshold for proving genocide so it could be used against America and its allies.

Mulvey rejected the claim as "misleading".

"The Gambia is very clear in its submissions; they are not asking the court to lower the threshold [for genocide]. Rather, they are saying the threshold has been met," she said.

What do the victims want?

Rohingya survivors want the court to find Myanmar responsible for genocide and to order the return of their land and property, compensation and prosecutions. 

Above all, they want citizenship, which they are denied under Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law, said Mulvey. 

If the court finds Myanmar responsible, it will also find that Myanmar must make reparation to the Rohingya, though it may defer the question of remedies to a later phase, Becker said.

The remedy the court orders "could be groundbreaking, especially if the ICJ requires Myanmar to undertake domestic reforms to guarantee basic rights of citizenship and non-discrimination to the Rohingya", he said.

"Decades on, they don't forget what has happened to them or to their families," Mulvey said. "At the very minimum, they want recognition."

What happens next?

Myanmar is bound to comply with the judgment. If it does not, the Gambia can refer the matter to the UN Security Council, which has never used its power to enforce an ICJ ruling.

Becker said enforcement may prove impossible while the military remains in power, but "compliance with the ICJ judgment may become the price of readmission to the international community". 

A finding against Myanmar could also increase pressure on other states to disengage from the ICJ, he said.

Myanmar has been embroiled in civil war since the 2021 coup, and the Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group, now controls most of Rakhine State.

Separately, the prosecutor of the International Criminal Court applied in November 2024 for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief, over the deportation and persecution of the Rohingya. Judges have not publicly ruled on the request.

“We want to see that arrest warrant issued, and also that arrest warrants are requested for other senior members of the Myanmar military,” Mulvey said.

In February 2025, a court in Argentina ordered arrest warrants for 25 Myanmar officials, including Min Aung Hlaing and Aung San Suu Kyi, in a case brought under the legal principle that atrocity crimes can be prosecuted anywhere. 

Because the court relies on precedents as part of its sources, the case will have implications on the other genocide-related cases pending before the ICJ: Ukraine v Russia, South Africa v Israel, Nicaragua v Germany and the Democratic Republic of the Congo v Rwanda.

item.title: Railway ticket crisis: A question of public service, accountability and governance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A basic question about public service arises from the apparent unavailability of train tickets from Dhaka to Sylhet for Friday, November 6.
Upaban Express (739) Dhaka departure 10pm, 6 November 2026; Sylhet arrival 5am, 7 November 2026. The displayed availability is zero for S_Chair, AC_B and Snigdha.
Jayentika Express (717) Dhaka departure 11:15 am, 6 November 2026; Sylhet arrival 7pm, 6 November 2026. The displayed availability is zero for AC_S, S_Chair and Snigdha.
Parabat Express (709) Dhaka departure 6:30am, 6 November 2026; Sylhet arrival 1pm, 6 November 2026. The displayed availability is zero for Snigdha, S_Chair and F_Seat.
Screenshots of the railway ticket-search page, captured on November 5, show zero available tickets in every class displayed for three services: Parabat Express, Jayentika Express, and Upaban Express. The situation is surprising enough to warrant a clear explanation from Bangladesh Railway.
Despite different departure times, the screenshots show zero available tickets in all the listed categories.
This raises an important question: Is the demand for travel to Sylhet on an ordinary Friday so exceptionally high that every listed seat on all three trains has been sold, or are there other factors affecting ticket availability?
The screenshots alone cannot establish whether all seats have genuinely been sold. Nor do they reveal how many passengers will actually board, how many tickets were allocated to different channels or quotas, or whether any technical or operational issue affected the online display. Those are precisely the questions that a transparent investigation should answer.
Bangladesh Railway should therefore verify the position on the ground. The Railway Secretary could form several effective inspection teams to examine the three Dhaka-Sylhet services.
The teams should compare the number of tickets issued with the number of passengers who actually board, check coach-wise occupancy, review quota and release arrangements, and examine whether tickets are being diverted, withheld or resold unlawfully.
The findings should be documented and made public, while protecting passengers’ personal information. If the investigation identifies irregularities or negligence, those responsible should face appropriate action under the applicable rules.
The issue also invites a wider reflection on the structure and performance of public institutions. Over time, railway administration has been given a dedicated department and then a separate ministry, with the associated senior administrative positions and public expenditure.
Institutional restructuring, however, should be judged by whether it improves the quality, reliability and accessibility of services -- not simply by the number of offices or senior posts created. The public is entitled to ask what measurable improvements have resulted from these changes.
The contrast with private transport is also worth examining. A passenger who approaches a private bus operator may sometimes find a seat for the following day, although the fare may be higher than the railway fare. This is not proof that private operators are always more efficient, or that railways can be assessed by exactly the same standards.
It does, however, highlight the importance of responsiveness, transparent booking, and reliable information. A public service should not leave passengers uncertain about whether tickets are genuinely sold out or simply unavailable through the channel they are using.
The answer is not necessarily to centralize every operational decision. Rather, Bangladesh needs clear central oversight, enforceable service standards, transparent ticket-allocation rules, reliable digital systems, and strong field-level monitoring.
Decentralized units must also be held to measurable performance targets. Where decentralization has weakened oversight or encouraged arbitrary practices, the arrangements should be reviewed and corrected.
Any reform -- centralized or decentralized -- must be based on evidence and must demonstrably improve public service.
There is also a public-finance dimension. When institutions fail to deliver the services expected of them, the state may face additional administrative costs, repeated interventions and avoidable losses.
Ultimately, public expenditure is funded by citizens, including through taxes. Preventing waste and ensuring that public officials perform their responsibilities are therefore not merely administrative concerns; they are matters of fairness to taxpayers.
The immediate request is straightforward: Let the Railway Secretary arrange an independent, practical check of the Dhaka-Sylhet trains and publish the findings.
Bangladesh Railway should explain how many tickets were released and sold, how many passengers travelled, whether all displayed seats were occupied, and whether any irregularity was found.
If the screenshots reflect genuine full occupancy, the public deserves accurate information about demand and capacity. If they do not, the reasons must be identified and corrected.
Citizens do not ask for institutions merely to exist; they expect them to serve. Public confidence in Bangladesh Railway will grow when ticketing is transparent, services are reliable, and responsibility is visible.
The real measure of governance is not the size of the administrative structure, but the quality of service experienced by ordinary people.
Md Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is a retired Additional Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration, Bangladesh.
