Why do women entrepreneurs struggle to secure loans?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh, getting a bank loan can mean confronting more than interest rates, paperwork, and eligibility requirements. The lending process does not simply involve bank officers and women in the SME sector.
A businesswoman seeking loans may also have to navigate a system shaped by assumptions about who belongs in business, who can handle financial matters, and who deserves to be taken seriously by government officers and other people involved in the lending process.
Although there is growing attention to facilitating women in funding their ventures in this country, gendered attitudes can make the loan application process a difficult and discouraging experience.
The case of guarantors for bank loans can illustrate the difficulty women face in accessing external funds for their small or medium businesses. Generally, loan applications require guarantors who satisfy particular conditions, such as being established businesspeople, government employees, or property owners.
When lending practices favour or expect male guarantors, women entrepreneurs may have difficulty identifying people within their professional and social networks who meet these requirements.
Women have had fewer opportunities to develop relationships with senior businesspeople, property owners, or officials due to their extensive workload at home and work or the patriarchal norms of having a distance from males in society.
Consequently, women entrepreneurs may have a smaller pool of people who can meet the bank's requirements or even struggle to find any of them.
The problem goes beyond the availability of potential guarantors. It can also reflect perceptions about women's credibility as business owners.
Given the gender stereotypical attitude, some potential guarantors may be reluctant to assume responsibility for a woman's business loan. Concerns about the legitimacy, stability, or financial prospects of a woman-owned business can make an already demanding requirement even more difficult to fulfil.
The collateral for bank loans is another powerful example to consider. As women in our society lack property, the collateral issue has received certain attention in the lending process.
While women have flexibility regarding collateral in applying for small amounts of loans, the case is complicated for seeking large loans. The problem is not restricted to simply not possessing property; it can be extended to providing necessary documents in banks to place collateral.
Obtaining these documents can involve interaction with land registration offices and other public institutions. Women may find themselves waiting longer, having difficulty obtaining assistance or feeling that their concerns are not taken as seriously as those of male applicants.
The issue is not necessarily that men receive uniformly favourable treatment. However, gender can add another layer of disadvantage for women when social expectations define business dealings, negotiation, and interaction with public officials as predominantly male activities.
Gender discrimination can take the form of subtle neglect, dismissive behaviour or an assumption that a woman is less capable of handling business-related matters independently.
This creates an additional burden for women seeking finance. A procedure that should be purely administrative can become an uncomfortable social encounter.
When women anticipate such treatment, some may become reluctant to approach public offices independently, thereby making the loan application process more complicated and time-consuming.
In short, when women encounter gender-biased attitudes during these processes, access to finance can become dependent not only on their business credentials but also on their ability to navigate gendered institutional environments.
As a result of such gendered problems, some women may seek smaller loans than they actually require, postpone expansion plans, rely on informal financing or avoid borrowing altogether.
Such outcomes matter not only for individual women entrepreneurs but also for the wider economy. When women-owned businesses cannot obtain adequate finance, opportunities for business expansion, employment creation, and income generation can also be constrained.
Improving women's access to credit therefore requires attention not only to the availability of financial products but also to the conditions under which those products are accessed.
Ensuring that women entrepreneurs can access formal finance requires removing not only the visible barriers written into loan procedures but also the less visible barriers created by social attitudes and institutional practices.
Banks need to design the lending process more critically to address the patriarchal problems associated with it. For instance, requirements concerning guarantors deserve careful consideration. Banks can examine whether particular requirements unintentionally disadvantage women entrepreneurs and whether alternative mechanisms can assess creditworthiness without unnecessarily restricting access to finance.
It is also important to take into account the social and institutional environment surrounding the lending process, which is not directly related to banks.
Public-sector employees need greater awareness of gender-sensitive service delivery. Women applicants should be treated consistently and respectfully, while procedures for documentation and communication should be sufficiently transparent that applicants do not have to depend on informal influence or personal connections.
Women's access to bank loans is not simply a question of whether a loan facility exists. It is also a question of whether women can enter the lending process on equal terms. In a deeply patriarchal society, dismantling the gendered obstacles will not be straightforward. Government agencies and financial institutions therefore need to work together to make lending practices more accessible, transparent, and responsive to women entrepreneurs.
Dr Jasmine Jaim is a Professor at Institute of Business Administration, Jahangirnagar University. She is an Associate Editor of the international journal Gender, Work and Organization, and social entrepreneur in the creative industry. The article has been developed based on the journal article “Bank loans access for women business-owners in Bangladesh: Obstacles and dependence on husbands” published in “Journal of Small Business Management.”

item.title: COP31: Another promise to the planet?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The longer the list of promises to save our planet grows, the faster the window of opportunity to address the climate crisis appears to be closing.
For more than three decades, world leaders have gathered at international climate conferences, announcing ambitious targets, establishing financial mechanisms, and pledging to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Yet rising global temperatures, extreme weather events, sea-level rise, and climate-related losses and damages have become increasingly alarming realities.
This persistent contradiction raises a fundamental question: Are new commitments truly driving meaningful change, or is each successive conference simply adding another layer of promises to those that remain unfulfilled?
The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) is scheduled to take place from November 9 to 20, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye. Türkiye will preside over the conference, while Australia will lead the formal negotiations.
The particular significance of this year's conference lies in its stated emphasis on implementing previous decisions alongside pursuing new commitments. However, understanding whether these expectations are realistic requires examining the historical evolution of international climate diplomacy.
1992-2015: From Rio to Paris, the historic journey of climate commitments
The institutional foundation of international climate cooperation was established through the adoption of the UNFCCC at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. Its underlying principle recognized that climate change is a global challenge, but countries differ in their historical responsibilities and capacities to address it.
The first Conference of the Parties, held in 1995, initiated a process of regular international climate negotiations. The Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997, established legally binding emissions-reduction targets for developed countries covered by its commitments. Although an important milestone, limited participation and implementation challenges constrained its effectiveness in controlling global emissions.
At the 2009 Copenhagen conference, developed countries committed to mobilizing $100 billion annually by 2020 to support climate action in developing countries. However, the target was not achieved within the agreed timeframe.
According to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), climate finance reached $115.9 billion in 2022, exceeding the annual target for the first time, two years after the agreed deadline. This delay further exposed the crisis of confidence between developed and developing countries in international climate negotiations.
The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, marked a historic turning point in climate diplomacy. Countries agreed to hold the increase in global average temperature well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. They also committed to submitting increasingly ambitious Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) every five years.
2021-2023: A new chapter in climate justice and energy transition
At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, countries collectively called for the phasedown of unabated coal power and the phaseout of inefficient fossil-fuel subsidies for the first time in a COP decision. The conference also reaffirmed the importance of strengthening climate adaptation and financial support.
However, no binding timetable was established for a complete transition away from fossil fuels. COP27, held in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt, in 2022, achieved an important breakthrough. Following prolonged negotiations, countries agreed to establish a Loss and Damage Fund to support vulnerable developing nations suffering from climate-related impacts.
For Bangladesh and other climate-vulnerable countries, this represented significant recognition of climate justice and the need to address damages associated with a crisis to which they have contributed relatively little.
At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, the first Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement was completed. The conference called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly, and equitable manner. It also highlighted the need to triple global renewable-energy capacity and double the global average annual rate of energy-efficiency improvement by 2030.
The decision to operationalize the Loss and Damage Fund was another important achievement. Nevertheless, the absence of clear, enforceable implementation obligations and adequate financial resources remained major limitations of these decisions.
COP29: New financial commitments, persistent implementation concerns
COP29, held in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, focused primarily on climate finance. After extensive negotiations, countries agreed on a new goal of mobilizing at least $300bn annually for developing countries by 2035, with developed countries taking the lead.
A broader objective of scaling climate finance from public and private sources to $1.3 trillion annually by 2035 was also advanced. Although the new financial target represented a substantial increase over the previous $100bn commitment, many developing countries considered it insufficient compared with their actual needs of climate adaptation, the transition to clean energy, and responses to climate-related losses and damages which require enormous financial investment.
Beyond the amount pledged, the nature of climate finance remains equally important. Loan-dependent assistance can increase the debt burden of climate-vulnerable countries. Therefore, grants, concessional financing, technology transfer, and accessible funding arrangements must receive greater attention.
The fundamental concern is whether these financial commitments will translate into timely and effective assistance for the countries and communities that need it most.
COP30: Familiar questions remained
COP30, held in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025, was presented as a conference focused on implementing climate commitments. Its location in the Amazon region highlighted the interconnections among forest conservation, biodiversity, and the global climate crisis.
The conference adopted the Belém Political Package. One of the key outcomes was an agreement calling for climate adaptation finance to be at least tripled by 2035, indicators for measuring progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, and initiatives such as the Global Implementation Accelerator and the Belém Mission to 1.5°C.
However, the collective outcome did not include a binding, time-bound roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. The Brazilian COP30 presidency subsequently initiated a separate process to develop relevant roadmaps.
Consequently, despite progress in negotiations, fundamental political disagreements over emissions reductions remained largely unresolved.
More concerningly, the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) 2025 assessment indicated that existing policies could result in approximately 2.8°C of global warming during this century.
Even if the latest national climate commitments were fully implemented, projected warming could remain between 2.3°C and 2.5°C. These estimates demonstrate that a considerable gap continues to exist between internationally agreed temperature goals and the actions required to achieve them.
COP31: A new era of implementation?
Against this background, the most important question facing COP31 is how previous commitments can be translated into practical action.
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires realistic country-specific implementation schedules, transparent progress assessments, and effective accountability mechanisms.
Similarly, announcing additional climate-finance targets will not be sufficient without examining actual financial delivery.
How much of the promised finance has been disbursed? What proportion has been provided as grants rather than loans? How much has reached vulnerable communities? These questions require transparent and measurable answers.
Strong international cooperation will also be essential for implementing the latest NDCs submitted around 2025. Meaningful progress will be difficult without balancing the historical responsibilities of developed countries, the development needs of emerging economies, and the principles of global climate justice.
COP31 should therefore become an opportunity to remove barriers to implementing earlier decisions rather than another competition to announce new commitments.
Bangladesh's expectations
Bangladesh contributes a relatively small share of global greenhouse gas emissions -- approximately 0.44% in 2024 -- yet remains highly exposed to multiple climate-related hazards.
Coastal salinity, cyclones, floods, droughts, riverbank erosion, and irregular rainfall increasingly threaten agriculture, water resources, infrastructure, and livelihoods.
According to Bangladesh's NDC 3.0, submitted in 2025, the country aims to reduce its projected greenhouse gas emissions by 20.31% by 2035 relative to a business-as-usual scenario.
This includes an unconditional reduction of 6.39% through domestic efforts and an additional conditional reduction of 13.92% dependent on international support.
Achieving these targets will require increased investment in renewable energy, efficient irrigation, climate-resilient agriculture, improved waste management, and technological capacity.
At the same time, easier access to adaptation finance and the Loss and Damage Fund remains essential. Bangladesh should therefore emphasize needs-based climate financing, grant-based assistance, technology transfer, and stronger international support for locally implementable adaptation projects.
For Bangladesh, climate diplomacy must ultimately deliver practical benefits to vulnerable populations rather than remain confined to international agreements.
The world needs action, not repeated promises
It would be unjustified to describe international climate conferences as complete failures. The Paris Agreement, the establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund, renewable-energy commitments, and climate-finance frameworks represent important achievements in international cooperation.
However, their effectiveness will ultimately depend on implementation. The success of COP31 should not be judged by the length of its final declaration, the number of newly announced commitments, or the financial figures presented at the negotiating table.
Instead, it should be measured by actual reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, climate finance reaching vulnerable communities, and demonstrable improvements in climate resilience.
The world does not need another layer of climate commitments. It needs credible evidence that existing promises are being fulfilled. Whether COP31 can initiate that transformation remains one of the most important questions facing global climate diplomacy.
Dr Md Shahjahan Kabir is Former Director General, BRRI.

item.title: An eye on food security. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Bangladesh Rice Research Institute's (BRRI) development of BRRI Dhan 119, a high-yielding, salt-tolerant rice variety, is a welcome achievement that deserves recognition and continued support.
With an average yield of 5.7 tons per hectare, and the potential to produce up to 7.6 tons under favourable conditions, the new variety offers considerable promise for farmers in coastal regions. It can tolerate significant levels of soil salinity, making it particularly valuable in areas where rising salinity has long restricted agricultural production.
Additionally, its shorter growing period of approximately 115 days has the potential to create opportunities to cultivate additional winter crops, including sunflower and salt-tolerant mustard, allowing farmers to make better use of their land.
This is particularly important as climate change continues to threaten Bangladesh's agricultural landscape. Rising sea levels, saltwater intrusion, and increasingly unpredictable weather patterns are putting pressure on traditional farming practices. Hence, developing resilient crop varieties is one of the most practical ways to protect agricultural productivity and strengthen long-term food security.
However, scientific achievements must translate into tangible benefits for farmers. Ensuring an adequate supply of quality seeds, making them affordable, and providing farmers with the necessary technical guidance will be crucial. Agricultural extension services must also help farmers understand the variety's suitability for different soil conditions and cultivation practices.
Research institutions should continue monitoring field performance and improving varieties to address emerging challenges.
Equally important is sustained investment in agricultural research. Our scientists have demonstrated that local expertise can produce solutions to distinctly local problems. Their work must receive consistent funding, institutional support, and opportunities for further innovation.
Food security cannot depend on production figures alone. It requires a resilient agricultural sector that can adapt to changing conditions while protecting farmers' livelihoods.
While BRRI Dhan 119 is a positive step in that direction, the challenge now is to ensure that this achievement reaches the fields and farmers who need it most.

item.title: We need better ways to raise revenue. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The National Board of Revenue’s decision to issue door-to-door notices to non-filing TIN holders may appear to widen the tax net, but is a strategy that risks becoming administrative pressure rather than meaningful reform.
The truth of the matter is that Bangladesh cannot build a stronger revenue system merely by sending notices to every name on a database.
In fact, the numbers point to a more basic problem: Of nearly 13 million TIN holders, only around five million filed returns in the previous fiscal year. Yet the NBR does not know how many remaining accounts belong to deceased people, individuals with no taxable income, or genuine defaulters.
Nearly 40% of notices are reportedly returned because addresses are outdated, while only 10% of recipients respond. Pursuing such records without first fixing the database is unlikely to generate substantial revenue.
The priority should be to modernize tax administration. The NBR needs an integrated, regularly updated database linked with civil registration and government records. It must make TIN cancellation and return submission simpler, improve digital services, and ensure taxpayers understand their obligations without unnecessary visits to tax offices.
Enforcement should focus on deliberate evasion, undisclosed wealth, and large-scale defaulters, rather than pressuring people who do not meet the income tax threshold.
More importantly, Bangladesh needs revenue targets that reflect economic realities and the capacity of its tax machinery. The NBR has repeatedly fallen short of ambitious targets, including a Tk41,879 crore deficit in the first quarter of FY27. Setting increasingly high figures without addressing structural weaknesses only creates pressure for hurried, ineffective collection drives.
Targets must be grounded in collection trends, economic growth and administrative capacity.
Revenue generation is essential to funding public services and development, but it requires public trust, fair enforcement, and a system that makes compliance easier.
The government must therefore pursue those reforms instead of relying on the current door-to-door notice system to compensate for unrealistic expectations.

item.title: Understanding the modern Bangladeshi. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Many Bangladeshis today can simultaneously feel deeply Muslim, strongly Bengali, and proudly Bangladeshi. Those identities are no longer necessarily perceived as mutually exclusive.
This synthesis did not happen overnight. It is the product of a century of political evolution, from the Muslim League to the Language Movement to the Liberation War, and a constitutional experiment that tried to codify it.
Bengali Muslim political thought was never identical to the North Indian Muslim League tradition. The two represented different answers to the same question: How should Muslims organize politically in colonial India?
In North India, from Sir Syed Ahmed Khan in the late 19th century to the All-India Muslim League founded in 1906, the emphasis was on Muslims as a minority needing educational modernization, constitutional safeguards, and eventually, recognition as a separate political nation. This trajectory culminated in the Lahore Resolution of 1940 and the creation of Pakistan in 1947.
In Bengal, there was a powerful alternative basis of identity: Bengali language, Bengali culture, and a territorial homeland. The political careers of A K Fazlul Huq, the Krishak Praja Party, and later the United Front illustrated this tendency. For the Bengali Muslim peasant, identity was simultaneously religious, linguistic, and territorial.
Thus, Bengali Muslim experience contained two competing concepts of identity: Muslim identity versus Bengali linguistic-cultural identity. After 1947, that tension became increasingly pronounced.
Pakistan’s attempt to impose Urdu as the sole state language produced the Language Movement of 1952. That movement was enormously important for the eventual development of Bangladeshi nationalism.
The Bengali Language Movement did something politically profound. It shifted the basis of collective identity from “we are Muslims living in Pakistan” toward “we are Bengalis whose language and culture constitute our collective identity.”
This did not eliminate Islam from Bengali identity. Rather, it separated religious identity from national-political identity. Religion remained central to personal and cultural life; language and culture became the basis of political nationality. That distinction eventually became fundamental to Bangladesh.
By the late 1960s and early 1970s, the Awami League’s political program under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman increasingly emphasized four principles: Bengali nationalism, democracy, economic justice (socialism), and secularism. The 1971 independence struggle transformed these from political slogans into the ideological foundations of a new state.
The Constitution of Bangladesh was adopted on November 4, 1972. Its preamble explicitly identified nationalism, socialism, democracy, and secularism as the fundamental principles of the Constitution. Article 8 made those four principles the fundamental principles of state policy.
But Article 12 gives us the most revealing definition of what the framers meant by secularism. It stated that secularism would be realized through elimination of:
That is extraordinarily significant. Bangladesh’s constitutional secularism was not primarily an attack on religion. It was principally an attack on using religion as the basis of political power and citizenship.
This is considerably closer to Indian-style constitutional secularism than to the more aggressively anti-clerical French model of laïcité.
The 1972 Constitution did not conceive secularism as “making Bangladesh a country without Muslims or without Islam.” Bangladesh was overwhelmingly Muslim from its birth.
Rather, the constitutional idea was that being Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, or Christian should not determine one’s political status as a Bangladeshi. That is why the original Article 12 simultaneously dealt with secularism and freedom of religion.
The conceptual vocabulary of secularism certainly came through the global modern political world, ultimately influenced by European Enlightenment thought, constitutionalism, and the American and French experiences. But the political reason Bangladesh adopted secularism was overwhelmingly indigenous.
It emerged from a specific Bengali experience: Muslim League politics → Pakistan → linguistic conflict → Bengali nationalism → 1971 Liberation War → 1972 Constitution.
And Article 12 tells us what the framers were trying to prevent: Religious communalism becoming the basis of political power.
There is one particularly interesting irony. The partition that created East Pakistan was supposed to solve the Hindu-Muslim political problem by separating the two communities geographically. But East Pakistan eventually demonstrated that Muslim identity alone was insufficient to overcome linguistic, cultural, and regional identity.
For many Bengali Muslims, 1947 created Pakistan, but 1971 created a political state in which being Bengali and being Muslim no longer had to be competing identities.
That makes it possible for a Bangladeshi Muslim today to look back at undivided Bengal and say: “I am glad Bangladesh exists, but I also feel that something precious was lost when Bengal was divided.”
That sentiment is not necessarily a rejection of Pakistan’s creation by their ancestors. It is often the result of seven decades of historical experience after Pakistan. Nostalgia for pre-1947 Bengal can coexist perfectly well with the creation of Bangladesh.
There is a fascinating demographic dimension to this. The enormous Hindu exodus from East Bengal and the much smaller but still substantial Muslim movement in the opposite direction fundamentally changed the social composition of both West Bengal and East Bengal.
The memories of those two migrations are very different -- and that helps explain why nostalgia for “undivided Bengal” is expressed differently by Bengali Hindus and Bengali Muslims.
For many West Bengali Hindus, undivided Bengal is a memory of a lost ancestral home. For many Bangladeshi Muslims, it is a cultural memory -- Tagore and Nazrul, Pahela Baishakh, bhatiali songs, traditional Bengali food -- without any desire to undo 1971.
Bangladesh’s experience after 1975 complicated the picture. The initial secular-nationalist period gave way to a gradual revival of Islamic political identity.
In 1977, Ziaur Rahman removed secularism as a fundamental principle and inserted Bismillah-ar-Rahman-ar-Rahim and a commitment to “absolute trust and faith in Almighty Allah.” In 1988, HM Ershad made Islam the state religion under Article 2A. In 2011, secularism was restored as a fundamental principle, but Bismillah and state religion were retained.
Bangladesh now has a constitution that simultaneously declares the state to be secular and Islam to be the state religion. That legal contradiction is the institutional expression of the identity synthesis described above -- a society that is overwhelmingly Muslim and yet determined that religion should not determine citizenship.
The fascinating historical irony is that Bangladesh’s secularism partly emerged from the failure of Pakistan’s Muslim-nationalist experiment to accommodate Bengali linguistic and cultural nationalism.
It was not an attempt to make Bangladesh less Muslim. It was an attempt to make Bangladesh a state where someone could admire Tagore and Nazrul, celebrate Bengali New Year, and at the same time identify strongly with Islam -- without one identity having to negate the other.

item.title: Top UN court to rule on Nov 19 on Myanmar's Rohingya genocide case. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The top United Nations court will on November 19 deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by The Gambia that Myanmar’s brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.

He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy which may be complicated by the ruling.

The judgement may also be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the decision by the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might sway in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar army and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.

More than one million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement.

‘Collective conscience’

During hearings on the case in January, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered “the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine”.

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction,” added the minister.

The Gambia has brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.

The alleged violations of the convention “are a stain on our collective conscience and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business”, Jallow said.

Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were “unsubstantiated”.

“Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts,” said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the president’s office.

In a previous hearing in 2019, de facto civilian leader Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.

The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingya’s expulsion and said there was no “genocidal intent” behind the crackdown.

Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, authorities say, after being unseated in the 2021 military coup.

The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to “take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts” described by the Genocide Convention.

These acts included “killing members of the group” and “deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part”.

ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.

The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.

A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.

item.title: Australia's Glenn Maxwell calls time on international career. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Explosive batsman Glenn Maxwell announced his international retirement Tuesday after being overlooked for Australia’s upcoming Twenty20 series against England.

The mercurial 38-year-old, who had not played a Test since 2017, called time on his one-day career last year but kept the door open for T20s.

He has not been picked since the World Cup in Sri Lanka in February, with selectors bypassing him for a series against Bangladesh in June.

Maxwell was again overlooked for the squad named Monday to play England in November, with a host of younger players instead preferred.

“A little bit sad and a little bit inevitable too, but I’m announcing my retirement from international cricket,” Maxwell said on the Final Word podcast.

“We probably had numerous discussions before and after the T20 World Cup,” he added of talks with selectors. “And it was pretty open-ended.

“There wasn’t any pressure from (Australia team management), and we decided to sort of leave the door open.

“There was a couple of series that were coming up (in which) they were going to look to the future, and we saw that in Bangladesh with guys getting their opportunity and performing really well.

“There was a small hope or discussion that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (against England).

“But I can completely understand the direction they’re going with this squad.” Maxwell played 130 T20 internationals, blasting 2,897 runs with a strike rate of 154.42, leaving as Australia’s third-highest run-scorer after David Warner and Aaron Finch.

While he only played seven Tests, he featured in 149 ODIs, crunching 3,990 runs.

Maxwell also called time on his first-class career with Victoria, but will continue with the Melbourne Renegades in the Big Bash League.

“I’m grateful for the time I was able to play for my country,” he said.

“If you had offered me that career when I first walked into the Victoria change rooms in 2009-ish, I would have bitten your hand off.”

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat, Hasan Nawaz named in Pakistan Shaheens squad for Rising Stars Asia Cup. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat and Hasan Nawaz have been included in the 15-member Pakistan Shaheens squad for the ACC Men’s Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026, with Abdul Samad appointed captain for the 50-over tournament to be held in Qatar from Nov 19 to 29.

The Pakistan Cricket Board announced the squad on Tuesday, with the Shaheens set to defend the title they won in the previous 50-over edition in 2023. Pakistan are also the defending champions of the T20 version of the competition, having beaten Bangladesh A in a final decided by a Super Over.

The eight-team tournament will feature two groups of four sides. Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside India A, Nepal and the United Arab Emirates, while Group ‘A’ comprises Afghanistan A, Bangladesh A, Hong Kong China and Sri Lanka A.

The Shaheens will open their campaign against the UAE on Nov 20, before taking on India A two days later and Nepal on Nov 24. Their first match will be played at the University of Doha Science and Technology ground, with the remaining group fixtures scheduled at the West End Park International Cricket Stadium.

All three group matches are day-night fixtures except the opening game, which will be played during the day. The semi-finals are scheduled for Nov 26 and 27, with the final to be held on Nov 29.

Samad will lead a batting group that includes Maaz, Hasan, Haider Ali, Shahzaib Khan, Farhan Yousuf and Shamyl Hussain. Rohail Nazir has been named as the designated wicket-keeper.

The squad also includes three spin options in left-arm spin all-rounder Danish Aziz, leg-spinner Saad Masood and Sufyan Moqim. The pace attack will be led by Mohammad Hasnain and also features Ahmed Daniyal, Akif Javed and Muhammad Imran Randhawa.

Ahmed Daniyal was part of the Shaheens side that won the previous T20 edition, playing a key role as the team clinched the title against Bangladesh A in a Super Over.

Pakistan won the last 50-over edition in Sri Lanka in 2023, beating India A by 128 runs in the final. They were runners-up in the opening two editions in 2013 and 2017 before winning the competition in 2019.

The Shaheens will be aiming to retain their title against a field that includes several of the region’s emerging sides, with a meeting against India A among the key fixtures in the group stage.

item.title: Beyond equality: The unfinished journey of women's rights in Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh's progress should be measured not only by economic growth, but by whether every woman and girl can live safely, learn, earn, speak and participate on equal terms.
A promise that must become everyday reality
Bangladesh has made important gains in girls' education and women's participation in public and economic life. Women work in factories, farms, schools, hospitals, businesses and public institutions; they support families and contribute to national development. Yet progress is not the same as equality. For many women, the ability to make choices about education, work, marriage, safety and public life is still constrained by violence, economic dependence and unequal expectations.
The Constitution provides a clear starting point. Articles 27 and 28 guarantee equality before the law and state that women have equal rights with men in all spheres of state and public life. The challenge is to make those guarantees real in homes, schools, workplaces, online spaces and public institutions.
The evidence on violence cannot be ignored
The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNFPA's Violence Against Women Survey 2024, published in October 2025, found that 76 per cent of women had experienced at least one form of intimate-partner violence in their lifetime, while 49 per cent experienced it in the previous 12 months. The survey also found that many survivors do not disclose the violence they experience. These figures are not simply statistics: they represent barriers to safety, health, dignity and equal participation.
A survivor may remain silent because of fear, stigma, financial dependence, pressure to preserve a marriage, concern for children or a lack of confidence that help will be available. Responses must therefore go beyond asking women to report abuse. Police, health services, legal-aid providers, local government and community organisations need to offer confidential, accessible and survivor-centred support. Investigations must be timely, protection must be practical, and accountability must not depend on a woman's income or social influence.
A childhood should not be cut short
Child marriage is another barrier to equality. UNICEF's Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025 preliminary findings report that 47.2 per cent of women aged 20–24 were first married before age 18. Behind this measure are girls whose education may be interrupted and whose choices about health, work and family life can narrow before adulthood.
Preventing child marriage requires more than enforcement after a marriage has been arranged. Families need social protection and economic support; schools must be safe and accessible; girls need quality secondary education and trusted adults to turn to. Community leaders and local institutions should challenge the idea that early marriage is a solution to poverty or insecurity. A girl's future should not be treated as a family burden to be transferred through marriage.
Economic participation must mean real opportunity
Women's economic contribution is substantial, but opportunity remains unequal. The World Bank's Gender Data Portal, using ILO modelled estimates, reports that female labour-force participation in Bangladesh was 38.6 per cent in 2025, compared with 80.4 per cent for men. Labour-force figures do not capture the full value of unpaid care and household work, much of which is performed by women. They do, however, point to a significant gap in participation in paid work and economic activity.
Closing that gap requires safe transport, affordable childcare, fair recruitment and promotion, equal pay for work of equal value, maternity protection, skills training and access to finance. Women working in informal and home-based sectors also need stronger protections. Entrepreneurship programmes should provide more than motivational messages: women need markets, mentoring, digital access, credit on fair terms and control over the income they earn.
Representation is not the same as influence
Women must be able to shape decisions, not merely appear in photographs or occupy positions without authority. Political parties, local government bodies, trade unions, professional associations and public institutions should create transparent pathways for women to lead. That includes protection from harassment and intimidation, fair access to resources, and meaningful roles in policy development.
Young women in particular should be encouraged to participate in community decision-making and public debate. Their presence can broaden the questions institutions ask and the solutions they consider. But representation should be judged by whether women can speak freely, influence priorities and be held to the same standards of accountability as everyone else.
A shared responsibility
Women's rights are not a concern for women alone. Men and boys, families, educators, employers, journalists, religious and community leaders, and public officials all have a role in challenging discrimination. Equality begins in ordinary decisions: whether a daughter is encouraged to continue her studies, whether care work is shared at home, whether harassment is taken seriously, and whether a woman's opinion is respected.
Bangladesh needs measurable commitments: reduce child marriage; strengthen prevention and response to gender-based violence; improve access to justice and support services; expand safe and decent work; and ensure women's meaningful participation in leadership. Progress should be tracked with reliable data and public reporting, including attention to rural women, women with disabilities, low-income households and women facing overlapping forms of exclusion.
The measure of progress
The unfinished journey of women's rights is not about granting special privileges. It is about ensuring that rights already recognized in law can be exercised in daily life. A girl should be able to finish school without being pushed into marriage. A woman should be able to work without harassment, earn without discrimination and seek justice without fear. She should be able to take part in public life without being threatened or silenced.
Bangladesh's future will be stronger when women's safety, freedom and equal opportunity are treated not as optional development goals, but as foundations of national progress. Equality is not achieved when it is promised. It is achieved when women can experience it—in every home, workplace, classroom and institution.
Shejuti Hossain is a writer and human rights activist.

item.title: From climate pledges to youth power: Bangladesh’s opportunity ahead of COP31. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In 2019, a group of law students in the Pacific began asking whether governments could be held accountable under international law for their response to climate change. Six years later, in July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion clarifying states’ climate obligations and responsibilities towards future generations. Young people had helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court.
Yet the money tells a different story. Between 2019 and 2021, youth-led climate justice initiatives received just 0.76% of mitigation-focused funding from some of the world’s largest climate foundations.
The contradiction is stark. Young people can influence international debates and national politics, yet struggle to secure the resources to turn their ideas into action. They are invited to conferences, consulted on policies and celebrated in public campaigns. But how much influence do they have over budgets, institutions and the decisions that determine where climate finance goes?
For Bangladesh, this is more than a question of representation. Generation Z played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape. As the country prepares for COP31, the challenge is to turn that civic influence into lasting institutional change.
Participation must lead to influence
Young people have spent years securing recognition within the UN climate process. YOUNGO, the official constituency for children and youth, gained full status in 2011. COP27 encouraged countries to include youth negotiators in national delegations, while COP28 established the Presidency Youth Climate Champion. At COP30 in Belém, youth consultations engaged thousands of participants.
These are worthwhile steps, but access does not guarantee influence. A conference badge cannot tell us whether young people changed a negotiating position, shaped a policy or influenced a budget. Travel costs, visa restrictions and limited observer places further disadvantage young people from least developed countries, small island developing states and climate-vulnerable communities.
The goal should be to connect participation with decisions, funding and measurable results.
Bangladesh has a foundation on which to build. Its National Adaptation Plan for 2023–2050 provides a long-term framework for climate resilience. Its NDC 3.0, submitted in 2025, includes child-sensitive targets for maintaining essential services during climate shocks. UNICEF has identified it as the first NDC globally to include youth in its measurement, reporting, and verification process.
The International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD) at Independent University, Bangladesh, has also demonstrated what practical support can achieve. Between 2023 and 2026, its SIDA-supported CAP-RES project trained 100 youth fellows and funded 57 youth-led climate sub-projects, which together directly reached 47,795 people, nearly half of them women. Such experience shows the value of combining training, mentoring and funding with community-level action.
Still, engagement remains fragmented and often dependent on individual projects and donor support. Opportunities are concentrated in urban centres, while young people from coastal areas, haors, chars and hill districts face greater barriers. Indigenous youth, young women and persons with disabilities need more equitable access. The agenda must also extend beyond adaptation to clean energy, mitigation and green skills, which will shape future employment.
Why climate finance misses young people
The problem is not simply a shortage of money. It is also how funding is designed and distributed.
A review of 100 youth-focused climate finance initiatives by the Commonwealth Secretariat and YOUNGO, launched at COP28, found that funding was generally disbursed in small amounts and information about beneficiaries was often inadequate.
Young applicants may lack established financial systems, organisational experience or evidence of results. Funders, however, also impose complex application requirements and short funding periods that can exclude smaller organisations. Conventional lenders may consider early-stage youth enterprises too risky.
Not every climate initiative should be expected to generate revenue. Community adaptation, disaster preparedness and climate research deliver public benefits that may not produce commercial returns. They need grants and public funding, not debt. Concessional loans, guarantees and blended finance have a role where youth-led enterprises have credible business models and realistic repayment prospects.
International commitments provide an opportunity, but access remains a concern. At COP29, developed countries committed to take the lead in mobilising at least US$300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, within a broader call to scale climate finance to US$1.3 trillion a year. COP30 called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035.
For least developed countries, the terms matter as much as the headline figures. The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, for example, had around US$250 million available for its first call for proposals, against requests estimated at US$2 billion to US$3 billion.
Least developed countries have also committed, through the LDC Initiative for Effective Adaptation and Resilience, to channel 70% of climate finance to local-level action by 2030. Youth-led initiatives should be part of this effort, supported by accessible funding channels and proportionate accountability requirements.
Turning commitments into action
Bangladesh does not need an entirely new climate finance system. It needs to make existing institutions more accessible and accountable.
First, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should formalise youth representation in NDC 3.0 monitoring, National Adaptation Plan reviews, local climate planning and official COP delegations. Selection should be transparent and geographically representative. Institutions should report annually on which youth recommendations were adopted and explain why others were not.
Second, national financing institutions should establish accessible funding windows. Bangladesh Bank could assess how its young entrepreneurs and green finance mechanisms might support viable youth-led climate enterprises. The Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund, Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation and Infrastructure Development Company Limited should create dedicated funding windows or explicitly include eligible youth-led initiatives in existing programmes.
Third, funding must match purpose. Grants should support research, community adaptation, disaster preparedness and early-stage testing. Repayable finance should be reserved for enterprises with credible cash flows. Mentoring, financial-management support and safeguards against excessive debt should accompany funding, with clear pathways for successful pilots to access further grants, public programmes or investment.
Fourth, the Finance Division and environment ministry should introduce a youth marker in annual climate budget reporting. Development partners and national financing institutions should distinguish commitments from actual disbursements. A regularly updated national mapping of youth climate organisations would help identify funding gaps and measure progress.
Fifth, international climate funds should strengthen Enhanced Direct Access, giving accredited National Implementing Entities the resources and authority to establish locally managed youth grant mechanisms. Simplified procedures should be balanced with appropriate technical support and financial oversight.
Finally, Bangladesh and the LDCs Group should use COP31 to press for an adequately resourced Action for Climate Empowerment plan that strengthens young people’s influence over climate decisions. They should also advocate for more accessible finance for locally led climate action and loss and damage, linked to clear national responsibilities and follow-up.
The opportunity in Antalya
Representation without funding leaves young people unable to act. Funding without transparent selection can reinforce existing inequalities. Both require institutions that explain how youth contributions influence decisions and what funded initiatives achieve.
Ahead of COP31 in Antalya this November, Bangladesh has an opportunity to move beyond expressions of support towards measurable commitments: Formal youth representation, accessible financing and transparent reporting. Its experience in climate planning and locally led adaptation gives it a credible basis for making that case.
Generation Z, which helped bring climate change before the world’s highest court in the Pacific and played a defining role in reshaping Dhaka’s political landscape, does not need another pavilion or another invitation to speak. It needs the authority to influence policy, the resources to put ideas into practice, and the means to hold decision-makers accountable.
Giving young people a genuine share of responsibility is not a symbolic gesture. It is a practical investment in those who will live longest with the consequences of decisions made today.

item.title: Seven migrants drown off Canary Islands. [ dawn ]
item.description:
MADRID: At least seven migrants died off Spain’s Canary Islands while more than 380 people were rescued on Monday, the country’s maritime rescue services said.

Two deceased people were found aboard a migrant boat when the coast guard rescued 132 people on Monday, 150 km off Lanzarote. During the same journey, five other migrants had died and been thrown into the sea, authorities added.

Another 250 migrants were rescued by coast guard boats off Lanzarote and the Canary Island of El Hierro earlier on Monday, authorities said. On Sunday, 107 migrants were rescued off El Hierro, according to authorities.

“The worst forecasts are coming true. The Atlantic route is once again claiming lives, this time off the coast of Lanzarote. Behind each one is a life, a story, and a family,” Canary Islands President Fernando Clavijo said in a message on X.

The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world’s deadliest migration crossings. Thousands of migrants attempt the journey each year in overcrowded boats, seeking to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances.

Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings.

Migrant arrivals have declined so far this year compared with the same period in 2025, but crossings increased sharply in October, putting additional pressure on reception and emergency services on some of the Canary Islands, particularly the smaller and less densely populated ones.

Migrant arrivals in the archipelago have fallen 18pc year on year to 11,527 people, according to the office of the Spanish government’s representative in the Canary Islands.

Asylum seekers deported

Spain has returned to Morocco more than a dozen sub-Saharan African and Asian migrants who reached the Spanish enclave of Ceuta and were turned down for asylum, the first deportation of its kind from the enclave since a mass border crossing in July.

The Interior Ministry said the group had been sent back to Morocco after it agreed to receive them and they remained on Moroccan territory at present. It declined to give numbers or nationalities but migrant and rights charities operating in Ceuta said 16 people from Senegal, Nigeria, Yemen, Cameroon and Bangladesh were deported.

The NGOs claim such returns fail to take into account the risks associated with Morocco’s treatment of migrants from other countries and fly in the face of the values espoused by Spain’s leftist government.

Virginia Alvarez, an Amnesty International researcher, said Spain’s posture was hypocritical. “Spain, despite its [progressive] speeches in Europe, is not ensuring that human rights guarantees are met for people who cross its borders in Ceuta and Melilla,” she said. “Morocco does not respect many human rights.”

item.title: The chars have no legal memory. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has a master plan for its haors . It has a distinctive legal and institutional framework for the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
But after more than two decades of working among the chars of the northern riverine areas, watching homes disappear into the river and reappear somewhere else, I still struggle to answer a simple question: Who is responsible for people who live on land that does not stay?
I have travelled for years through the char areas of Kurigram and Gaibandha, along the Jamuna and Brahmaputra.
I have watched families dismantle their homes for the third or fourth time in a decade -- tin sheets pulled down, bamboo bundled, chickens loaded onto boats -- often without knowing where they will rebuild next.
Bangladesh has built specific institutions and programs for other fragile geographies. In 2000, it established the Bangladesh Haor and Wetland Development Board, followed by a 20-year Haor Master Plan in 2012.
The Chittagong Hill Tracts, meanwhile, have a distinctive legal and institutional framework rooted in the 1900 Regulation, the 1997 Peace Accord, and the 1998 Regional Council Act.
Photo: Courtesy
The chars are different. Bangladesh does have programs such as the Char Development and Settlement Project, which has worked on infrastructure, livelihoods and land settlement in newly accreted chars.
But there is still no dedicated statutory framework for a basic reality that erosion-prone char communities face repeatedly: The land can physically disappear, communities can be displaced, and the administrative identity attached to a place can disappear with it.
Our institutions are largely designed for land that stays put. Registration, schools, health facilities, local government records, and land administration become extraordinarily complicated when the land itself is moving.
When a char disappears, it is not only houses that go with it.
I have seen villages where the school, the madrasa, the tube-well and other community facilities vanished into the river in a single season. It is not several separate disasters. It is one settlement disappearing at once.
I worked with these communities for years and witnessed their repeated displacement firsthand.
The inhabitants of Sidhai Char, under Mollarchar Union, have had to shift their entire settlement more than once -- not just their homes, but also the school and an NGO-run weaving centre that had provided local women with a rare source of income.
An entire ecosystem of livelihoods and community life had to be dismantled and rebuilt because nothing could remain anchored to the land once the river took it away.
In nearby Dewanganj, river erosion has also threatened and swallowed schools and other community infrastructure. But at least some communities manage to move together. Some chars do not offer even that possibility.
I think often of Sirajbeg, a char in Kurigram that no longer exists. The river did not simply erode its edges; it eventually took the whole char.
Photo: Courtesy
There was no single relocation and no common destination. Its people scattered to other chars, upazilas and districts across the north -- and, for families I know personally, as far as Dhaka.
They did not resettle as a community. They dispersed as individuals, each finding their own way to survive.
Ask them where they are from, and they will say Sirajbeg.
But Sirajbeg is no longer on the map in the way it once was.
There may be no functioning local institution tied to the vanished settlement, no surviving school record readily accessible to every family, and no land document that every displaced household can produce to establish what it once owned.
What remains is memory -- and memory alone is rarely enough at a land office or government counter.
A community like Sidhai's can lose its buildings and still retain much of its social fabric because it moves together.
A community like Sirajbeg's can lose both the land and the community itself, leaving people scattered across different places and holding records that may no longer reflect where they came from.
When a char reforms, the community does not simply return. It starts again, often without a single institution responsible for helping it do so.
For years, we have advised char families to keep their NID, birth registration, and land documents together and carry them whenever they move. It is sensible advice.
But imagine a family fleeing a collapsing riverbank at night, with children and livestock to save and perhaps one boat available. Is it realistic to expect them to remember a folder of papers?
Sometimes those papers go into the river too.
And even when documents survive, another question remains: Which institution will recognize the family's connection to the place it has left behind?
For a family whose home, school, and local community infrastructure disappeared together, the challenge is immense.
This is not simply a housing issue. It is a question of legal identity, land rights and access to citizenship and public services.
In December 2025, the International Organization for Migration, working with the government of Bangladesh and development partners, released the country's first comprehensive nationwide estimate of disaster-induced internal displacement.
It estimated that 4,955,527 people were currently internally displaced because of natural disasters. The assessment covered all eight divisions, 64 districts, and thousands of local administrative units. A large share of those displaced had been displaced for years rather than only during a recent emergency.
Bangladesh is not starting from zero. The country adopted a national strategy on disaster- and climate-induced internal displacement in 2015 and a broader National Strategy on Internal Displacement Management in 2021. A National Action Plan for implementing that strategy covers 2022-2042.
Programs such as Ashrayan have also provided housing and rehabilitation to hundreds of thousands of landless and homeless families. The Char Development and Settlement Project has worked for decades to improve livelihoods, infrastructure and land settlement in vulnerable char areas.
But a house is not legal identity, and resettlement is not necessarily a secured land claim.
A family can receive a new roof and still struggle to establish its previous land rights. It can be counted as resettled and still move again when the next erosion event arrives.
Its children may have birth registration and NID records, yet the administrative memory of the community they came from can gradually disappear.
This is the gap we need to address.
The river does not simply take land. It can take the administrative memory of a community.
Photo: Courtesy
As Bangladesh considers its next phase of development and climate-adaptation priorities, it should consider creating a dedicated institutional mechanism for the rights and administrative continuity of char communities.
Such a body would not replace existing char-development programmes. Instead, it could fill the gap between development, land administration, legal protection and internal displacement.
It could maintain digital and physical records of land claims that survive relocation; preserve the original identity of vanished settlements; maintain duplicate civil and community records; provide legal assistance to families contesting land and inheritance claims; coordinate services when communities relocate together; and help trace families when a settlement is dispersed across chars, districts or cities.
Most importantly, it could create a system of portable legal and administrative identity for people whose geography is not portable.
The goal is not simply to move people from one place to another.
It is to ensure that when the river takes their land, it does not also take their rights.
Somewhere in Dhaka today, a family may still call itself the people of Sirajbeg -- a char that exists nowhere except in what they remember.
The chars have no legal memory. It is time Bangladesh gave them one.
Ahmed Toufiqur Rahman is a rotarian and development professional with 24 years of experience. Email: thetoufiqrahman@gmail.com .

item.title: An unsavoury tug of war. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the self-declared return date of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina draws closer, discussion of the Awami League in Bangladesh’s political arena keeps growing. The party that those in power have declared “irrelevant,” is the very party they have now started a tug of war over.
On one side, BNP alleges that Jamaat-e-Islami is striking an understanding with them. On the other, Jamaat counter-alleges that BNP is scheming to bring the Awami League back into politics.
Although the Awami League was excluded from the February general election, the field stayed heated with discussion about whom its supporters would vote for, why they would vote for them, or whether they would vote at all. That discussion continues even after the voting. BNP leaders like to say that Awami League supporters voted for Jamaat.
The latest chapter of pointing fingers at each other was started by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman himself at a public rally in Rajshahi last month. “There is clear intelligence information that the autocrat who fled is supplying money there. Whom are they helping by supplying this money? There are some people, a party, who spread confusion in the country. Who tried to sell various tickets to the public before the election, telling lies. These two sides have become one.”
‘Autocrat’ and ‘ticket seller’
Needless to say, by “autocrat” the PM meant the Awami League, and by the party that “sold tickets” before the election, he meant Jamaat-e-Islami. Jamaat not only rejected this allegation but also made a counter-allegation that BNP came to power by striking an understanding with the Awami League. It is worth mentioning here, though, that even though eight months of the BNP government has passed, no result of this alleged understanding with the Awami League is yet visible.
Both parties claim to be the torchbearers of the 2024 anti-government movement, and day in and day out, they pledge to resist the Awami League’s return to politics. But from their recent talk, it appears that a large part of their politics is taken up by the party that was ousted in 2024.
Awami League leaders are saying that they will not cooperate with any party, whether BNP, Jamaat, or NCP. They want to convey that the ideological gap between the Awami League and these parties is so great that there is no question of an understanding among them.
On the other hand, in the backdrop of Bangladesh’s politics, the possibility of an “understanding” between the Awami League and either Jamaat or BNP cannot be ruled out entirely. A glance at the past shows that just as Jamaat has adopted various kinds of strategies to survive, in exactly the same way, the two big parties have used Jamaat to hurt each other.
It is often understood that Jamaat was rehabilitated in independent Bangladesh with the cooperation of General Ziaur Rahman and his party, BNP. But later the Awami League too did not hesitate to cooperate with Jamaat.
For example, in the 1986 election, the League and Jamaat participated when the other anti-Ershad parties, including BNP, boycotted the vote. The two parties conducted their anti-Ershad movement in coordination with Jamaat, although they refrained from giving Jamaat a place on their own platform. In the country’s politics there was still something called a sense of shame ( chokkhulojja ) then.
Jamaat in Khaleda’s cabinet
Jamaat’s relationship with BNP began to grow close after Ershad’s fall. Although BNP contested the 1991 election alone, many suspected at that time that an unwritten “understanding” had been reached with Jamaat. Although the BNP won the election, it did not get the seats necessary to form a government. After Jamaat’s 18 MPs extended their support, BNP was able to form the government.
A decade after the first cabinet of Khaleda Zia, BNP and Jamaat formally formed an alliance and jointly took part in the 2001 election. By then the sense of shame of the eighties and nineties had bid farewell to the country.
Having won the election, two former commanders of the Al-Badr force, Motiur Rahman Nizami and Ali Ahsan Mohammad Mujahid, got places in Khaleda Zia’s new cabinet.
The Awami League too has worked together with Jamaat to put BNP in a difficult position. The biggest example of this is the 1994 incident in which the two parties resigned from parliament together, demanding elections under a caretaker government. The two parties conducted the anti-BNP movement together, although outside parliament they never came onto one stage. The Awami League’s sense of shame was still maintained then.
BNP’s relationship with Jamaat is deep. They have contested elections in one alliance and formed a government together. They have agitated together and carried out violence across the country, including arson ( jalao-pora , “burn and torch”).
The Awami League has cooperated with Jamaat at certain times for strategic reasons, but in elections or on the streets, the leaders and activists of these two parties were not seen together.
Now the question is: In the present backdrop of politics, how likely is an “understanding” between the Awami League and Jamaat?
Anti-Awami unity
The prime minister spoke of “intelligence” information. Through this statement, it became known that the intelligence agencies have again become active in the political arena, collecting information on opposition parties. But have the intelligence agencies really given this information? And if they have, did they supply correct information, or are they arranging their briefs to serve the government’s current agenda?
The prime minister did not present any evidence in support of his statement, but merely saying “intelligence has information” is also not enough. This is especially so since, from 2001 onward, only BNP’s name was being added to Jamaat’s.
After the 2024 change of power, in the absence of the Awami League, the Jamaat sees itself as BNP’s rival for power. BNP too is getting the chance to shoot fish in a barrel. Neither of these two parties wants the Awami League to return to politics. They do not want it in their own interests. Opposition to the Awami League holds these two parties together in a kind of unity.
Jamaat probably sees the announcement of Sheikh Hasina’s return as a sign of some understanding behind the scenes. Along with them, the young leaders of NCP have also become somewhat restless over the Awami League question.
The protests, including long marches, by Jamaat and NCP in various regions of the country, are being held for the implementation of the July Charter. It can be assumed that another aim of this program is to keep up pressure so that the government does not become lenient towards the Awami League.
Awami League’s challenge
The war of words between BNP and Jamaat-NCP is now at the stage of the boxing “shadow fight.” The two sides are circling each other but are not trying to land a blow. If an understanding with the Awami League were proven, it would amount to betrayal of 2024. But through this, they are once again proving how relevant the Awami League is in Bangladesh’s politics.
For the Awami League’s leaders, the biggest challenge now is to hold the party together and to lift the morale of leaders and activists. There are three most important goals before them now. First, how Sheikh Hasina’s return to the homeland can be made successful. Second, lifting the ban on the Awami League’s activities. And third, freeing their leaders and activists from jail and settling the cases filed against them.
Why would the Awami League make an understanding with Jamaat to achieve these goals? None of these goals seems achievable with Jamaat’s help. It is foolish even to think that Jamaat would help the Awami League achieve its goals.
But BNP may perhaps think, and the intelligence agencies may perhaps have fed that thinking, that the Awami League’s aim is to create anarchy in the country and put the government in danger by weakening Tarique Rahman’s hand and force him to become lenient towards the Awami League. But even there, the possibility of an Awami League-Jamaat understanding is slim.
The Awami League needs to reach an understanding with the government, because it is through this understanding that Sheikh Hasina’s return can become possible and safe. Likewise, it is through an understanding with the government that the path for the Awami League’s return to politics can be smoothed. In reaching an understanding with the government, mediation by some third force will be needed, since BNP and the Awami League have stopped even seeing each other’s faces.
Sabir Mustafa is the former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the author’s own.
